title: What is TypeScript and how does it relate to JavaScript?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational TypeScript (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: TypeScript is a strongly typed programming language developed by Microsoft that builds on JavaScript by adding optional static typing.: Syntactic Superset: Any valid JavaScript code is automatically valid TypeScript code (.js files can be renamed to .ts) • Compile-Time Only: Browsers and Node.js cannot execute TypeScript directly.

title: What are Primitive Types vs Object Types in TypeScript?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational TypeScript (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: Primitive Types: Built-in immutable JavaScript primitives: string, number, boolean, bigint, symbol, null, undefined • Object Types: Non-primitive structures: object, arrays (number[]), interfaces, classes, tuples, and functions • Convention Note: Always use lowercase primitive types (string, number, boolean).

title: Compare `any`, `unknown`, and `never`.
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational TypeScript (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: Type Meaning Type Safety Operations Allowed.

title: What is the difference between `type` alias and `interface`?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational TypeScript (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: Both define the shape of objects, but they have key architectural differences.

title: How do Function Signatures and Return Types (`void` vs `never`) work?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational TypeScript (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: void: Indicates a function completes execution without returning a value (returns undefined implicitly) • never: Indicates a function never finishes successfully—either it throws an uncaught exception or enters an infinite loop (while(true)).

title: Why does modern TypeScript favor String Union Types over Enums?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational TypeScript (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: Numeric and standard Enums in TypeScript generate real JavaScript code during compilation (creating reverse-mapping object tables).: Enums: Pollute the compiled bundle with runtime object overhead and can produce unsafe numeric assignments (enum Status { Active, Inactive }).

title: What are Tuples and `as const` assertions?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational TypeScript (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: Tuple: An array with a fixed length and known types at specific indices: [string, number] • as const (Const Assertion): Tells the compiler to infer the most specific, literal, readonly type possible.

title: What is the difference between Type Assertions (`as`) and Type Casting?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational TypeScript (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: Type Casting in languages like C# or Java converts data representations at runtime (e.g. converting float bytes to integer) • Type Assertion (as Type) in TypeScript is purely a compile-time instruction telling the compiler: "Trust me, I know the type better than you.

title: What is Structural Typing (Duck Typing)?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational TypeScript (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: TypeScript uses structural typing, not nominal typing. Two types are considered identical if they have the same structure (shape), regardless of their declared names.

title: What are Generics and why are they necessary?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational TypeScript (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: Generics allow you to write reusable, type-safe functions, classes, and interfaces that work over a variety of types rather than a single fixed type, capturing the argument type dynamically.

title: How do Generic Constraints (`extends`) work?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational TypeScript (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: By default, generic T can be anything. Using T extends Shape constrains T to types that contain specific required properties.

title: What is the `keyof` operator and Indexed Access types?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational TypeScript (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: keyof T: Produces a union of all property keys of type T • T[K] (Indexed Access): Extracts the type of a specific property K on type T.

title: What are Discriminated Unions (Tagged Unions)?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational TypeScript (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: A pattern where multiple object types share a common, unique literal property (the "discriminant" or "tag"). TypeScript automatically narrows the union inside a switch or if block.

title: How do Type Narrowing and Custom Type Guards (`is`) work?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational TypeScript (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: TypeScript automatically narrows types within conditional branches using: typeof x === 'string' • x instanceof Date • 'property' in obj.

title: What are the essential flags in `tsconfig.json`?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational TypeScript (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: "strict": true: Enables all strict type-checking options (the single most important flag) • "target": "ES2022": Target ECMAScript version for output JS • "module": "NodeNext": Module system for code generation • "noImplicitAny": true: Raises an error on any variable whose type defaults to any.

title: What are Conditional Types and Distributive Conditional Types?
part: Part 2: Advanced Type System & Metaprogramming (Mid-Level)
summary: Conditional types choose one of two possible types based on a subtyping relationship: T extends U ? X : Y.

title: How does the `infer` keyword work in conditional types?
part: Part 2: Advanced Type System & Metaprogramming (Mid-Level)
summary: infer allows you to declare a type variable inside the condition to extract or unwrap an unknown subtype.

title: What are Mapped Types and Key Remapping (`as`)?
part: Part 2: Advanced Type System & Metaprogramming (Mid-Level)
summary: Mapped types build new types by transforming each property in an existing type.

title: What are Template Literal Types?
part: Part 2: Advanced Type System & Metaprogramming (Mid-Level)
summary: Template literal types bring JavaScript template string interpolation syntax directly into the type system.

title: Explain Standard Utility Types: `Partial`, `Required`, `Readonly`, `Record`.
part: Part 2: Advanced Type System & Metaprogramming (Mid-Level)
summary: PartialT: Makes all properties optional (?) • RequiredT: Removes all optional modifiers (-?) • ReadonlyT: Adds readonly to all properties • Record: Constructs an object type with property keys K and value type T.

title: Explain Filtering Utility Types: `Pick`, `Omit`, `Exclude`, `Extract`.
part: Part 2: Advanced Type System & Metaprogramming (Mid-Level)
summary: Pick: Constructs a type by picking specific keys K from object T • Omit: Constructs a type by omitting keys K from object T • Exclude: Excludes from union T all members assignable to U • Extract: Extracts from union T all members assignable to U.

title: What is the `satisfies` operator in TypeScript 4.9+?
part: Part 2: Advanced Type System & Metaprogramming (Mid-Level)
summary: Before satisfies, you had a dilemma: If you annotated const palette: Colors = { .. • If you omitted the annotation const palette = { .

title: How do you implement a Deep Partial or Deep Readonly type?
part: Part 2: Advanced Type System & Metaprogramming (Mid-Level)
summary: Standard PartialT is shallow (only makes top-level keys optional). Using recursive conditional types, we can make every nested level optional.

title: What are Overloaded Function Signatures?
part: Part 2: Advanced Type System & Metaprogramming (Mid-Level)
summary: Function overloading allows a function to accept different combinations of parameters and return different types. You define multiple public function signatures followed by a single private implementation.

title: What are Ambient Declarations and `.d.ts` files?
part: Part 2: Advanced Type System & Metaprogramming (Mid-Level)
summary: Ambient declarations describe the shape of existing JavaScript code that has no built-in types (e.g., globals on window, external C-modules, or legacy npm packages). Defined using the declare keyword in .d.ts files. They contain zero executable JavaScript—only type definitions.

title: What are `const` Type Parameters (TypeScript 5.0+)?
part: Part 2: Advanced Type System & Metaprogramming (Mid-Level)
summary: In TypeScript 5.0, you can prefix a generic parameter with const to enforce that calls automatically infer as const literal types without forcing callers to write as const manually!

title: What is Variance in TypeScript (Covariance vs Contravariance)?
part: Part 2: Advanced Type System & Metaprogramming (Mid-Level)
summary: Variance describes how subtyping of complex types relates to subtyping of their component types: Covariance (Output positions): If Dog extends Animal, then Dog[] extends Animal[], and () => Dog extends () => Animal • Contravariance (Input/Parameter positions): Function parameters are contravariant under strictFunctionTypes.

title: What is the `asserts` condition operator?
part: Part 2: Advanced Type System & Metaprogramming (Mid-Level)
summary: The asserts keyword defines an assertion function. If the function returns without throwing, TypeScript narrows the type of the argument for all subsequent lines in that scope.

title: What are Excess Property Checks?
part: Part 2: Advanced Type System & Metaprogramming (Mid-Level)
summary: TypeScript normally allows passing an object with extra properties where fewer properties are expected (structural typing). However, when passing an object literal directly, TypeScript triggers Excess Property Checks to prevent typos.

title: How do ECMAScript Stage 3 Decorators work in TypeScript 5.x?
part: Part 2: Advanced Type System & Metaprogramming (Mid-Level)
summary: TypeScript 5.0 adopted the official ECMAScript standard Decorators (replacing the legacy experimentalDecorators flag). Decorators are functions applied to classes, methods, accessors, and fields to wrap or replace them.

title: Explain the TypeScript Compiler Architecture and Compilation Pipeline.
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Compiler Internals & Performance (Senior / Staff)
summary: The tsc compiler operates across five sequential stages: Scanner: Reads source text and converts characters into Tokens • Parser: Consumes tokens and builds the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) • Binder: Traverses the AST and connects declarations to Symbols (scoping and symbol table) • Checker: The core of TypeScript.

title: How do you implement Nominal Typing (Branded Types) in TypeScript?
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Compiler Internals & Performance (Senior / Staff)
summary: Because TypeScript is structurally typed, a UserId (string) and an OrderId (string) are completely interchangeable, leading to catastrophic runtime bugs where an order ID is passed into a user deletion function! Branded Types attach a unique compile-time phantom property.

title: How do you optimize TypeScript compilation speed in massive enterprise codebases?
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Compiler Internals & Performance (Senior / Staff)
summary: skipLibCheck: true: Skips type-checking of all .d.ts declaration files inside node_modules (saves up to 50% compilation time) • incremental: true: Saves compilation state to a .tsbuildinfo cache file for fast incremental builds.

title: What are Project References and Composite Projects?
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Compiler Internals & Performance (Senior / Staff)
summary: In a monorepo with 50 packages, running tsc across all 50 packages in a single run exhausts memory and takes minutes.

title: How does Runtime Validation (Zod) synchronize with Compile-Time TypeScript?
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Compiler Internals & Performance (Senior / Staff)
summary: TypeScript types vanish at runtime and cannot validate incoming API payloads from external users. Zod provides runtime schema validation that automatically infers static TypeScript types using z.infer.

title: How do you build a strongly-typed Event Emitter?
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Compiler Internals & Performance (Senior / Staff)
summary: By mapping event names to their payload types, you can enforce that emit and on require exact payload signatures.

title: How do you diagnose and debug slow types in a TypeScript codebase?
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Compiler Internals & Performance (Senior / Staff)
summary: Complex recursive conditional types or massive union combinations can freeze tsc.: Run tsc --extendedDiagnostics: Displays total check time, number of types created, and memory usage • Run tsc --generateTrace trace_dir: Generates Chrome DevTools performance traces.

title: What causes the error `Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite`?
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Compiler Internals & Performance (Senior / Staff)
summary: TypeScript caps recursive type evaluations (around 1,000 recursive steps in modern versions) to prevent compiler stack overflows.: Cause: Recursive mapped types lacking a proper base case or operating over circular data structures.

title: Explain TypeScript Module Resolution Modes (`Node16`, `NodeNext`, `Bundler`).
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Compiler Internals & Performance (Senior / Staff)
summary: Node16 / NodeNext: Adheres strictly to Node.js ESM rules (requires explicit file extensions in imports like import './utils.js', respects • Bundler: Introduced in TS 5.0 for modern bundlers (Vite, Webpack, Turbopack) that resolve extensions and paths without requiring .js extensions.

title: What is the difference between `declare module` and `declare global`?
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Compiler Internals & Performance (Senior / Staff)
summary: declare module "some-package": Augments or provides types for an external npm package • declare global: Augments the top-level global environment (adding properties to window, globalThis, or document) from within a module file.

title: How do you enforce Exhaustive Type Checking in `switch` statements?
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Compiler Internals & Performance (Senior / Staff)
summary: Assigning the unhandled case to a never variable guarantees that if a new member is added to a union, the TypeScript compiler will fail until all cases are handled.

title: What is the difference between Method Signatures and Property Signatures in Interfaces?
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Compiler Internals & Performance (Senior / Staff)
summary: ```typescript interface Comparer { method(a: number): void; // Bivariant (under strictFunctionTypes) property: (a: number) => void; // Contravariant (strictly checked) }.

part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Compiler Internals & Performance (Senior / Staff)
summary: By default with strict: true, an optional property foo?: string allows assigning foo = undefined. Enabling "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true enforces that an optional property must either be present with the exact type (foo: "hello") or completely omitted ({}), but never explicitly assigned undefined.

part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Compiler Internals & Performance (Senior / Staff)
summary: TypeScript provides the ts.transform API allowing compiler plugins to inspect and modify AST nodes during compilation: Walks the AST using ts.visitEachChild • Detects specific nodes (e.g. ts.isCallExpression).

title: What is the recommended strategy for migrating a 500k-line legacy JS codebase to strict TS?
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Compiler Internals & Performance (Senior / Staff)
summary: Enable TypeScript in loose mode: Set "allowJs": true, "checkJs": false, "strict": false • Setup CI with --noEmit: Type check files without generating build assets • Migrate leaf files first: Convert utilities and core constants (.js -> .ts).

title: How do you write Type-Safe SQL queries with Kysely or Slonik?
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Compiler Internals & Performance (Senior / Staff)
summary: Instead of ORMs that hide SQL or raw strings with zero type checking, type-safe query builders like Kysely use TypeScript's mapped and indexed access types: Database schema is defined as a TypeScript interface • Kysely's query builder autocompletes table and column names and infers the exact return type of SELECT expressions.

title: What are the flagship innovations introduced in TypeScript 5.0 through 5.5+?
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Compiler Internals & Performance (Senior / Staff)
summary: TS 5.0: Standard ECMAScript Decorators, const type parameters, multiple config inheritance (extends: [...]) • TS 5.1: Unrelated types for getters and setters, decoupled JSX namespaces for React Server Components • TS 5.2: using declarations (Explicit Resource Management / Disposable pattern).

title: What is Angular Framework?
part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)
summary: Angular is a TypeScript-based open-source front-end platform that makes it easy to build web, mobile and desktop applications. The major features of this framework include declarative templates, dependency injection, end to end tooling which ease application development.

title: What is the difference between AngularJS and Angular?
part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)
summary: AngularJS (version 1.x) is a JavaScript framework, whereas Angular (version 2+) is a complete rewrite of AngularJS using TypeScript, providing better performance, mobile support, modularity, and a more modern architecture.

title: What is TypeScript?
part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)
summary: TypeScript is a strongly typed superset of JavaScript created by Microsoft that adds optional types, classes, async/await and many other features, and compiles to plain JavaScript. Angular is written entirely in TypeScript as a primary language.

title: What are directives?
part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)
summary: Directives add behaviour to an existing DOM element or an existing component instance.

part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)

title: What is a template?
part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)
summary: A template is a HTML view where you can display data by binding controls to properties of an Angular component. You can store your component's template in one of two places.

title: What is a module?
part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)
summary: Modules are logical boundaries in your application and the application is divided into separate modules to separate the functionality of your application.

title: What is a data binding?
part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)
summary: Data binding is a core concept in Angular and allows to define communication between a component and the DOM, making it very easy to define interactive applications without worrying about pushing and pulling data. There are four forms of data binding(divided as 3 categories) which differ in the way the data is flowing.

title: What is metadata?
part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)
summary: Metadata is used to decorate a class so that it can configure the expected behavior of the class. The metadata is represented by decorators.

title: What is the difference between constructor and ngOnInit?
part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)
summary: The Constructor is a default method of the class that is executed when the class is instantiated and ensures proper initialisation of fields in the class and its subclasses.

title: What is a service?
part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)
summary: A service is used when a common functionality needs to be provided to various modules. Services allow for greater separation of concerns for your application and better modularity by allowing you to extract common functionality out of components.

title: What is dependency injection in Angular?
part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)
summary: Dependency injection (DI), is an important application design pattern in which a class asks for dependencies from external sources rather than creating them itself.

title: How is Dependency Hierarchy formed?
part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)
summary: Injectors in Angular have rules that can be leveraged to achieve the desired visibility of injectables in your applications. By understanding these rules, you can determine in which NgModule, Component, or Directive you should declare a provider.

title: What is the purpose of async pipe?
part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)
summary: The AsyncPipe subscribes to an observable or promise and returns the latest value it has emitted. When a new value is emitted, the pipe marks the component to be checked for changes.

title: What is the option to choose between inline and external template file?
part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)
summary: You can store your component's template in one of two places. You can define it inline using the template property, or you can define the template in a separate HTML file and link to it in the component metadata using the @Component decorator's templateUrl property.

title: What is the purpose of *ngFor directive?
part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)
summary: Angular templates provide iterative rendering to display collections of items. You can render collections using either the Classic Built-in Structural Directive (ngFor) or the modern Built-in Control Flow (@for)** introduced in Angular 17+.

title: What is the purpose of *ngIf directive?
part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)
summary: Angular provides conditional rendering to show or hide portions of the DOM based on a truthy/falsy condition. You can implement conditional rendering using the Classic Built-in Structural Directive (ngIf) or the modern Built-in Control Flow (@if)** introduced in Angular 17+.

title: What happens if you use script tag inside template?
part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)
summary: Angular recognizes the value as unsafe and automatically sanitizes it, which removes the script tag but keeps safe content such as the text content of the script tag. This way it eliminates the risk of script injection attacks. If you still use it then it will be ignored and a warning appears in the browser console.

title: What is interpolation?
part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)
summary: Interpolation is a special syntax that Angular converts into property binding. It’s a convenient alternative to property binding. It is represented by double curly braces({{}}). The text between the braces is often the name of a component property. Angular replaces that name with the string value of the corresponding component property.

title: What are template expressions?
part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)
summary: A template expression in Angular produces a value similar to any JavaScript expression. Angular executes the expression during change detection and assigns the computed result to a property of a binding target—such as an HTML element attribute, a component @Input(), or a directive property.

title: What are template statements?
part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)
summary: A template statement responds to an event raised by a binding target, such as an HTML element, component output (@Output()), or directive. Template statements appear in quotes to the right of the (event) symbol in event binding syntax: (event)="statement".

title: How do you categorize data binding types?
part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)
summary: Binding types can be grouped into three categories distinguished by the direction of data flow. They are listed as below: From the source-to-view • From view-to-source • View-to-source-to-view.

part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)

part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)

title: What are observables?
part: Part 1: Architecture, Components, Directives & Lifecycle (1 - 35)
summary: Observables are declarative which provide support for passing messages between publishers and subscribers in your application. They are mainly used for event handling, asynchronous programming, and handling multiple values. In this case, you define a function for publishing values, but it is not executed until a consumer subscribes to it.

title: What are different types of compilation in Angular?
part: Part 4: JIT vs AOT Compilation, Metadata & TypeScript (76 - 100)
summary: Angular offers two ways to compile your application: Just-in-Time (JIT) • Ahead-of-Time (AOT).

title: What is JIT?
part: Part 4: JIT vs AOT Compilation, Metadata & TypeScript (76 - 100)
summary: Just-in-Time (JIT) is a type of compilation that compiles your app in the browser at runtime. JIT compilation was the default until Angular 8, now default is AOT.

title: What is AOT?
part: Part 4: JIT vs AOT Compilation, Metadata & TypeScript (76 - 100)
summary: Ahead-of-Time (AOT) is a type of compilation that compiles your app at build time. This is the default starting in Angular 9.

title: Why do we need compilation process?
part: Part 4: JIT vs AOT Compilation, Metadata & TypeScript (76 - 100)
summary: The Angular components and templates cannot be understood by the browser directly. Due to that Angular applications require a compilation process before they can run in a browser. For example, In AOT compilation, both Angular HTML and TypeScript code converted into efficient JavaScript code during the build phase before browser runs it.

title: What are the advantages with AOT?
part: Part 4: JIT vs AOT Compilation, Metadata & TypeScript (76 - 100)
summary: Faster rendering: The browser downloads a pre-compiled version of the application • Fewer asynchronous requests: It inlines external HTML templates and CSS style sheets within the application javascript which eliminates separate • Smaller Angular framework download size: Doesn't require downloading the Angular compiler.

title: What are the ways to control AOT compilation?
part: Part 4: JIT vs AOT Compilation, Metadata & TypeScript (76 - 100)
summary: You can control your app compilation in two ways: By providing template compiler options in the tsconfig.json file • By configuring Angular metadata with decorators.

title: What are the restrictions of metadata?
part: Part 4: JIT vs AOT Compilation, Metadata & TypeScript (76 - 100)
summary: In Angular, You must write metadata with the following general constraints: Write expression syntax with in the supported range of javascript features • The compiler can only reference symbols which are exported • Only call the functions supported by the compiler • Decorated and data-bound class members must be public.

title: What are the three phases of AOT?
part: Part 4: JIT vs AOT Compilation, Metadata & TypeScript (76 - 100)
summary: The AOT compiler works in three phases: Code Analysis: The compiler records a representation of the source • Code generation: It handles the interpretation as well as places restrictions on what it interprets.

title: Can I use arrow functions in AOT?
part: Part 4: JIT vs AOT Compilation, Metadata & TypeScript (76 - 100)

title: What is the purpose of metadata json files?
part: Part 4: JIT vs AOT Compilation, Metadata & TypeScript (76 - 100)
summary: The metadata.json file can be treated as a diagram of the overall structure of a decorator's metadata, represented as an abstract syntax tree(AST).

title: Can I use any javascript feature for expression syntax in AOT?
part: Part 4: JIT vs AOT Compilation, Metadata & TypeScript (76 - 100)
summary: No, the AOT collector understands a subset of (or limited) JavaScript features. If an expression uses unsupported syntax, the collector writes an error node to the .metadata.json file. Later point of time, the compiler reports an error if it needs that piece of metadata to generate the application code.

title: What is folding?
part: Part 4: JIT vs AOT Compilation, Metadata & TypeScript (76 - 100)
summary: The compiler can only resolve references to exported symbols in the metadata. Where as some of the non-exported members are folded while generating the code.

part: Part 4: JIT vs AOT Compilation, Metadata & TypeScript (76 - 100)
summary: Metadata rewriting is the process in which the compiler converts the expression initializing the fields such as useClass, useValue, useFactory, and data into an exported variable, which replaces the expression. Remember that the compiler does this rewriting during the emit of the .js file but not in definition files( .d.ts file).

title: What is React?
part: General
summary: React (aka React.js or ReactJS) is an open-source front-end JavaScript library for building user interfaces based on components. It's used for handling the view layer in web and mobile applications, and allows developers to create reusable UI components and manage the state of those components efficiently.

title: What is the history behind React evolution?
part: General
summary: The history of ReactJS started in 2010 with the creation of XHP. XHP is a PHP extension which improved the syntax of the language such that XML document fragments become valid PHP expressions and the primary purpose was used to create custom and reusable HTML elements.

title: What are the major features of React?
part: General
summary: React offers a powerful set of features that have made it one of the most popular JavaScript libraries for building user interfaces.

title: What is JSX?
part: General
summary: JSX stands for JavaScript XML and it is an XML-like syntax extension to ECMAScript. Basically it just provides the syntactic sugar for the React.createElement(type, props...children) function, giving us expressiveness of JavaScript along with HTML like template syntax.

title: What is the difference between an Element and a Component?
part: General
summary: Think of elements as the instructions for creating UI, and components as reusable blueprints that combine logic and structure to generate those instructions.

title: How to create components in React?

summary: Components are the building blocks of creating User Interfaces(UI) in React. There are two possible ways to create a component.

title: What are Pure Components?
part: General
summary: Pure components are the components which render the same output for the same state and props. In function components, you can achieve these pure components through memoi.

title: What is state in React?
part: General
summary: State of a component is an object that holds some information that may change over the lifetime of the component. The important point is whenever the state object changes, the component re-renders. It is always recommended to make our state as simple as possible and minimi.

title: What are props in React?
part: General
summary: Props are inputs to components. They are single values or objects containing a set of values that are passed to components on creation similar to HTML-tag attributes. Here, the data is passed down from a parent component to a child component.

title: What is the difference between state and props?
part: General
summary: In React, both state and props are plain JavaScript objects, but they serve different purposes and have distinct behaviors.

title: What is the difference between HTML and React event handling?
part: General
summary: In HTML, the event name usually represents in lowercase as a convention.

title: What are synthetic events in React?
part: General
summary: SyntheticEvent is a cross-browser wrapper around the browser's native event. Its API is same as the browser's native event, including stopPropagation() and preventDefault(), except the events work identically across all browsers. The native events can be accessed directly from synthetic events using nativeEvent attribute.

title: What are inline conditional expressions?
part: General
summary: You can use either if statements or ternary expressions which are available in JS(and JSX in React) to conditionally execute or render expressions. Apart from these approaches, you can also embed any expressions in JSX by wrapping them in curly braces and then followed by JS logical operator &&.

title: What is "key" prop and what is the benefit of using it in arrays of elements?
part: General
summary: A key is a special attribute you should include when mapping over arrays to render data. Key prop helps React identify which items have changed, are added, or are removed.

title: What is Virtual DOM?
part: General
summary: The Virtual DOM (VDOM) is a lightweight, in-memory representation of Real DOM used by libraries like React to optimi.

title: How Virtual DOM works?
part: General
summary: The Virtual DOM works in five simple steps.

title: What is the difference between Shadow DOM and Virtual DOM?
part: General
summary: The Shadow DOM is a browser technology designed primarily for scoping variables and CSS in web components. The Virtual DOM is a concept implemented by libraries in JavaScript on top of browser APIs.

title: What is React Fiber?
part: General
summary: React Fiber is the new reconciliation engine in React, introduced in React 16. It’s a complete rewrite of React’s core algorithm(old stack-based algorithm) for rendering and updating the UI. Fiber enhances React’s ability to handle asynchronous rendering, **prioriti.

title: What is the main goal of React Fiber?
part: General
summary: The goal of React Fiber is to increase its suitability for areas like animation, layout, and gestures. Its headline feature is incremental rendering: the ability to split rendering work into chunks and spread it out over multiple frames.

title: What are controlled components?
part: General
summary: A controlled component is a React component that fully manages the form element's state(e.g, elements like , , or )) using React's internal state mechanism. i.e, The component does not manage its own internal state — instead, React acts as the single source of truth for form data.

title: What are uncontrolled components?
part: General
summary: The Uncontrolled components are form elements (like , , or ) that manage their own state internally via the DOM, rather than through React state. You can query the DOM using a ref to find its current value when you need it. This is a bit more like traditional HTML.

title: What is the difference between createElement and cloneElement?
part: General
summary: Both React.createElement and React.cloneElement are used to work with React elements, but they serve different purposes.

title: What is Lifting State Up in React?
part: General
summary: When several components need to share the same changing data then it is recommended to lift the shared state up to their closest common ancestor. That means if two child components share the same data from its parent, then move the state to parent instead of maintaining local state in both of the child components.

title: What are Higher-Order Components?
part: General
summary: A higher-order component (HOC) is a function that takes a component and returns a new enhanced component with additional props, behavior, or data. It’s a design pattern based on React’s compositional nature, allowing you to reuse logic across multiple components without modifying their internals.

title: What is children prop?
part: General
summary: The children prop is a special prop in React used to pass elements between the opening and closing tags of a component. It is commonly used in layout and wrapper componnents.

title: How to write comments in React?
part: General
summary: The comments in React/JSX are similar to JavaScript Multiline comments but are wrapped in curly braces.

title: What is reconciliation?
part: General
summary: Reconciliation is the process through which React updates the Browser DOM and makes React work faster. React use a diffing algorithm so that component updates are predictable and faster. React would first calculate the difference between the real DOM and the copy of DOM (Virtual DOM) when there's an update of components.

title: Does the lazy function support named exports?
part: General
summary: No, React.lazy currently supports default exports only. If the component you want to import is exported using named exports, you can create an intermediate module that re-exports it as the default, or resolve it using .then() on the dynamic import promise.

title: Why React uses className over class attribute?
part: General
summary: React uses className instead of class because of a JavaScript naming conflict with the class keyword.

title: What are fragments?
part: General
summary: It's a common pattern or practice in React for a component to return multiple elements. Fragments let you group a list of children without adding extra nodes to the DOM. You need to use either Fragment or a shorter syntax having empty tag (<>).

title: Why fragments are better than container divs?
part: General
summary: Fragments are a bit faster and use less memory by not creating an extra DOM node • Some CSS mechanisms like Flexbox and CSS Grid have a special parent-child relationships, and adding divs in the middle makes it hard to keep the • The DOM Inspector is less cluttered.

title: What are portals in React?
part: General
summary: A Portal is a React feature that enables rendering children into a DOM node that exists outside the parent component's DOM hierarchy, while still preserving the React component hierarchy. Portals help avoid CSS stacking issues—for example, elements with position: fixed may not behave as expected inside a parent with transform.

title: What are stateless components?
part: General
summary: If the behaviour of a component is independent of its state then it can be a stateless component. You can use either a function or a class for creating stateless components. But unless you need to use a lifecycle hook in your components, you should go for function components.

title: What are stateful components?
part: General
summary: If the behaviour of a component is dependent on the state of the component then it can be termed as stateful component. These stateful components are either function components with hooks or class components.

title: How to apply validation on props in React?
part: General
summary: When the application is running in development mode, React will automatically check all props that we set on components to make sure they have correct type. If the type is incorrect, React will generate warning messages in the console. It's disabled in production mode due to performance impact.

title: What are the advantages of React?
part: General
summary: Increases the application's performance with Virtual DOM • JSX makes code easy to read and write • It renders both on client and server side (SSR) • Easy to integrate with frameworks (Angular, Backbone) since it is only a view library.

title: What are the limitations of React?
part: General
summary: React is just a view library, not a full framework • There is a learning curve for beginners who are new to web development • Integrating React into a traditional MVC framework requires some additional configuration • The code complexity increases with inline templating and JSX.

title: What are the recommended ways for static type checking?
part: General
summary: Modern Recommendation (2026): TypeScript is the industry standard for type checking in React applications.

title: What is the use of react-dom package?
part: General
summary: The react-dom package provides DOM-specific methods that can be used at the top level of your app. Most of the components are not required to use this module. Some of the methods of this package are: render() • hydrate() • unmountComponentAtNode() • findDOMNode().

title: What is ReactDOMServer?
part: General
summary: The ReactDOMServer object enables you to render components to static markup (typically used on node server). This object is mainly used for server-side rendering (SSR). The following methods can be used in both the server and browser environments: renderToString() • renderToStaticMarkup().

title: How to use innerHTML in React?
part: General
summary: The dangerouslySetInnerHTML attribute is React's replacement for using innerHTML in the browser DOM. Just like innerHTML, it is risky to use this attribute considering cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks. You just need to pass a __html object as key and HTML text as value.

title: How to use styles in React?
part: General
summary: The style attribute accepts a JavaScript object with camelCased properties rather than a CSS string. This is consistent with the DOM style JavaScript property, is more efficient, and prevents XSS security holes.

title: How events are different in React?
part: General
summary: Handling events in React elements has some syntactic differences: React event handlers are named using camelCase, rather than lowercase • With JSX you pass a function as the event handler, rather than a string.

title: What is the impact of indexes as keys?
part: General
summary: Keys should be stable, predictable, and unique so that React can keep track of elements.

title: How do you conditionally render components?
part: General
summary: In some cases you want to render different components depending on some state. JSX does not render false or undefined, so you can use conditional short-circuiting to render a given part of your component only if a certain condition is true.

title: Why we need to be careful when spreading props on DOM elements?
part: General
summary: When we spread props we run into the risk of adding unknown HTML attributes, which is a bad practice. Instead we can use prop destructuring with ...rest operator, so it will add only required props.

title: How do you memoize a component?
part: General
summary: In React, you can memoize a functional component using React.memo(). It wraps your component to prevent unnecessary re-renders if its props have not changed (via shallow comparison).

title: How you implement Server Side Rendering or SSR?
part: General
summary: React is already equipped to handle rendering on Node servers. A special version of the DOM renderer is available, which follows the same pattern as on the client side.

title: How to enable production mode in React?
part: General
summary: You should use Webpack's DefinePlugin method to set NODE_ENV to production, by which it strip out things like propType validation and extra warnings. Apart from this, if you minify the code, for example, Uglify's dead-code elimination to strip out development only code and comments, it will drastically reduce the si.

title: Do Hooks replace render props and higher order components?
part: General
summary: Both render props and higher-order components render only a single child but in most of the cases Hooks are a simpler way to serve this by reducing nesting in your tree.

title: What is a switching component?
part: General
summary: A switching component is a component that renders one of many components. We need to use object to map prop values to components.

title: What are the Pointer Events supported in React?
part: General
summary: Pointer Events provide a unified way of handling all input events. In the old days we had a mouse and respective event listeners to handle them but nowadays we have many devices which don't correlate to having a mouse, like phones with touch surface or pens.

title: Why should component names start with capital letter?

title: What is Next.js, and how does it extend standard React?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational Concepts (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: Standard React (Vite / CRA): A client-side library • Next.js: A production full-stack React framework • Server-Side Rendering (SSR) & Static Site Generation (SSG): Pre-renders HTML on the server • React Server Components (RSC): Runs components exclusively on the server, shipping 0KB of JS to the client.

title: What are the key differences between the App Router (`app/`) and the legacy Pages Router (`pages/`)?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational Concepts (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: Feature Legacy Pages Router (pages/) Modern App Router (app/).

title: What is Server-Side Rendering (SSR) vs. Static Site Generation (SSG) vs. Client-Side Rendering (CSR)?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational Concepts (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: CSR (Client-Side Rendering): Empty HTML sent; browser fetches data and renders everything • SSG (Static Site Generation): HTML is generated once at build time (next build) • SSR (Server-Side Rendering): HTML is generated on the server dynamically on every incoming HTTP request.

title: What is Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR) and how does `revalidate` work?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational Concepts (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: Historically, SSG required rebuilding the entire website whenever content changed in a CMS. ISR allows you to update static pages in the background without rebuilding the whole site.

title: What are React Server Components (RSC) and how do they differ from Client Components?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational Concepts (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: In Next.js App Router, all components are React Server Components by default: RSC (Server Components) • Execute only on the server • Can directly query databases (db.query()), access server files (fs), and use sensitive secrets (process.env.API_SECRET).

title: When should you use the `'use client'` directive?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational Concepts (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: You only need to add 'use client' at the top of a file when the component requires: React hooks: useState, useReducer, useEffect, useRef • Interactive DOM event listeners: onClick, onChange, onSubmit • Browser APIs: window, document, navigator, localStorage • Custom hooks that depend on client state or context providers.

title: What are Server Actions in Next.js (`'use server'`)?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational Concepts (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: Server Actions are asynchronous server functions that can be called directly from Client or Server components without manually creating REST API endpoints.

title: How does File-Based Routing work in the App Router?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational Concepts (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: Special reserved filenames inside app/ define the UI hierarchy: page.tsx: Makes the route publicly accessible and defines its unique UI • layout.tsx: Shared UI wrapping the page and its child routes.

summary: JavaScript provides two types of equality operators: Loose equality (==, !=): Performs type conversion if the types differ, comparing values after converting them to a common type • Strict equality (===, !==): Compares both value and type, without any type conversion.

title: What are lambda expressions or arrow functions
part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: Arrow functions (also known as "lambda expressions") provide a concise syntax for writing function expressions in JavaScript. Introduced in ES6, arrow functions are often shorter and more readable, especially for simple operations or callbacks.

title: What is a first class function
part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: In JavaScript, first-class functions(first-class citizens) mean that functions are treated like any other variable. That means: You can assign a function to a variable • You can pass a function as an argument to another function • You can return a function from another function.

title: What is a first order function
part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: A first-order function is a function that doesn’t accept another function as an argument and doesn’t return a function as its return value. i.e, It's a regular function that works with primitive or non-function values.

title: What is a higher order function
part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: A higher-order function is a function that either accepts another function as an argument, returns a function as its result, or both. This concept is a core part of JavaScript's functional programming capabilities and is widely used for creating modular, reusable, and expressive code.

title: What is a unary function
part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: A unary function (also known as a monadic function) is a function that accepts exactly one argument. The term "unary" simply refers to the function's arity—the number of arguments it takes.

title: What is the currying function
part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: Currying is the process of transforming a function with multiple arguments into a sequence of nested functions, each accepting only one argument at a time.

title: What is a pure function
part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: A pure function is a function whose output depends only on its input arguments and produces no side effects. This means that given the same inputs, a pure function will always return the same output, and it does not modify any external state or data.

title: What are the benefits of pure functions
part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: Some of the major benefits of pure functions are listed below: Easier testing: Since output depends only on input, pure functions are simple to test • Predictability: No hidden side effects make behavior easier to reason about.

title: What is the purpose of the let keyword
part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: The let keyword in JavaScript is used to declare a block-scoped local variable. This means that variables declared with let are only accessible within the block, statement, or expression where they are defined.

title: What is the reason to choose the name let as a keyword
part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: The keyword let was chosen because it originates from mathematical notation, where "let" is used to introduce new variables (for example, "let x = 5"). This term was adopted by several early programming languages such as Scheme and BASIC, establishing a tradition in computer science.

title: What is the Temporal Dead Zone
part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: The Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) refers to the period between the start of a block and the point where a variable declared with let or const is initialized. During this time, the variable exists in scope but cannot be accessed, and attempting to do so results in a ReferenceError.

summary: encodeURI() function is used to encode an URL. This function requires a URL string as a parameter and return that encoded string. decodeURI() function is used to decode an URL. This function requires an encoded URL string as parameter and return that decoded string.

title: What is memoization
part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: Memoization is a functional programming technique which attempts to increase a function’s performance by caching its previously computed results. Each time a memoized function is called, its parameters are used to index the cache. If the data is present, then it can be returned, without executing the entire function.

title: What is Hoisting
part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: Hoisting is JavaScript's default behavior where variable and function declarations are moved to the top of their scope before code execution. This means you can access certain variables and functions even before they are defined in the code.

part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: In ES6, JavaScript classes are primarily syntactic sugar over JavaScript’s existing prototype-based inheritance. For example, the prototype based inheritance written in function expression as below.

title: What are closures
part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: A closure is the combination of a function bundled(enclosed) together with its lexical environment within which that function was declared. i.e, It is an inner function that has access to the outer or enclosing function’s variables, functions and other data even after the outer function has finished its execution.

title: What are modules
part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: Modules refer to small units of independent, reusable code and also act as the foundation of many JavaScript design patterns. Most of the JavaScript modules export an object literal, a function, or a constructor.

title: What is scope in javascript
part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: Scope is the accessibility of variables, functions, and objects in some particular part of your code during runtime. In other words, scope determines the visibility of variables and other resources in areas of your code.

title: What is a service worker
part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: A Service worker is basically a script (JavaScript file) that runs in the background, separate from a web page and provides features that don't need a web page or user interaction.

title: How do you manipulate DOM using a service worker
part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: Service worker can't access the DOM directly. But it can communicate with the pages it controls by responding to messages sent via the postMessage interface, and those pages can manipulate the DOM.

title: How do you reuse information across service worker restarts
part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: The problem with service worker is that it gets terminated when not in use, and restarted when it's next needed, so you cannot rely on global state within a service worker's onfetch and onmessage handlers. In this case, service workers will have access to IndexedDB API in order to persist and reuse across restarts.

title: What is IndexedDB
part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: IndexedDB is a low-level API for client-side storage of larger amounts of structured data, including files/blobs. This API uses indexes to enable high-performance searches of this data.

title: What is web storage
part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: Web storage is an API that provides a mechanism by which browsers can store key/value pairs locally within the user's browser, in a much more intuitive fashion than using cookies. The web storage provides two mechanisms for storing data on the client.

title: What is a post message
part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: Post message is a method that enables cross-origin communication between Window objects.(i.e, between a page and a pop-up that it spawned, or between a page and an iframe embedded within it).

part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)

title: Why do you need a Cookie
part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: Cookies are used to remember information about the user profile(such as username). It basically involves two steps: When a user visits a web page, the user profile can be stored in a cookie • Next time the user visits the page, the cookie remembers the user profile.

part: Part 1: Core Objects, Prototypes, Functions & Scope (1 - 53)
summary: Web storage is more secure, and large amounts of data can be stored locally, without affecting website performance. Also, the information is never transferred to the server. Hence this is a more recommended approach than Cookies.

title: What is a promise
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: A Promise is a JavaScript object that represents the eventual completion (or failure) of an asynchronous operation and its resulting value. It acts as a placeholder for a value that may not be available yet but will be resolved in the future.

title: Why do you need a promise
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: Promises are used to handle asynchronous operations, especially in languages like JavaScript, which often work with non-blocking operations such as network requests, file I/O, and timers. When an operation is asynchronous, it doesn't immediately return a result; instead, it works in the background and provides the result later.

title: Explain the three states of promise
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: Promises have three states: Pending: This is an initial state of the Promise before an operation begins • Fulfilled: This state indicates that the specified operation was completed • Rejected: This state indicates that the operation did not complete.

part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)

title: What are the main rules of promise
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: A promise must follow a specific set of rules: A promise is an object that supplies a standard-compliant .then() method • A pending promise may transition into either fulfilled or rejected state • A fulfilled or rejected promise is settled and it must not transition into any other state.

title: What is callback in callback
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: You can nest one callback inside in another callback to execute the actions sequentially one by one. This is known as callbacks in callbacks. Beware, too many levels of nesting lead to Callback hell.

part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)

title: What is promise.all
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: Promise.all() is a built-in JavaScript method used to handle multiple asynchronous operations together. It accepts an iterable of promises (usually an array) and returns a single promise that resolves only when all the input promises have successfully resolved.

title: Does Promise.all() cancel the other Promises?
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: No. Promise.all() does not cancel the other promises. It only waits for all of them to finish, and if any one rejects, the overall Promise.all() call rejects immediately.

part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)

title: What is a strict mode in javascript
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: JavaScript’s "use strict" directive is used to opt into a stricter parsing and error-handling mode for your scripts or functions. It helps catch common bugs, makes your code more secure, and prepares it for future versions of JavaScript.

title: Why do you need strict mode
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: Strict mode is useful to write "secure" JavaScript by notifying "bad syntax" into real errors. For example, it eliminates accidentally creating a global variable by throwing an error and also throws an error for assignment to a non-writable property, a getter-only property, a non-existing property, a non-existing variable, or a...

title: How do you declare strict mode
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: The strict mode is declared by adding "use strict"; to the beginning of a script or a function. If declared at the beginning of a script, it has global scope.

title: What is the purpose of the delete operator
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: The delete operator is used to delete the property as well as its value.

title: What is typeof operator
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: You can use the JavaScript typeof operator to find the type of a JavaScript variable. It returns the type of a variable or an expression.

title: What is undefined property
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: The undefined property indicates that a variable has not been assigned a value, or declared but not initialized at all. The type of undefined value is undefined too.

title: What is null value
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: The value null represents the intentional absence of any object value. It is one of JavaScript's primitive values. The type of null value is object. You can empty the variable by setting the value to null.

summary: The eval() function evaluates JavaScript code represented as a string. The string can be a JavaScript expression, variable, statement, or sequence of statements.

summary: The window.history object contains the browser's history. You can load previous and next URLs in the history using back() and next() methods.

title: How do you detect caps lock key turned on or not
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: The mouseEvent getModifierState() is used to return a boolean value that indicates whether the specified modifier key is activated or not. The modifiers such as CapsLock, ScrollLock and NumLock are activated when they are clicked, and deactivated when they are clicked again.

title: What is isNaN
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: The isNaN() function is used to determine whether a value is an illegal number (Not-a-Number) or not. i.e, This function returns true if the value equates to NaN. Otherwise it returns false.

title: What are global variables
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: Global variables are those that are available throughout the length of the code without any scope. The var keyword is used to declare a local variable but if you omit it then it will become global variable.

title: What are the problems with global variables
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: The problem with global variables is the conflict of variable names of local and global scope. It is also difficult to debug and test the code that relies on global variables.

title: What is NaN property
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: The NaN property is a global property that represents "Not-a-Number" value. i.e, It indicates that a value is not a legal number. It is very rare to use NaN in a program but it can be used as return value for few cases.

title: What is the purpose of isFinite function
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: The isFinite() function is used to determine whether a number is a finite, legal number. It returns false if the value is +infinity, -infinity, or NaN (Not-a-Number), otherwise it returns true.

title: What is an event flow
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: Event flow refers to the order in which events are handled in the browser when a user interacts with elements on a webpage like clicking, typing, hovering, etc.

title: What is event capturing
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: Event capturing is a phase of event propagation in which an event is first intercepted by the outermost ancestor element, then travels downward through the DOM hierarchy until it reaches the target (innermost) element.

title: What is event bubbling
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: Event bubbling is a type of event propagation in which an event first triggers on the innermost target element (the one the user interacted with), and then bubbles up through its ancestors in the DOM hierarchy — eventually reaching the outermost elements, like the document or window.

title: How do you submit a form using JavaScript
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: You can submit a form using document.forms[0].submit(). All the form input's information is submitted using onsubmit event handler.

title: How do you find operating system details
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: The window.navigator object contains information about the visitor's browser OS details. Some of the OS properties are available under platform property.

title: What is the difference between document load and DOMContentLoaded events
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: The DOMContentLoaded event is fired when the initial HTML document has been completely loaded and parsed, without waiting for assets(stylesheets, images, and subframes) to finish loading. Whereas The load event is fired when the whole page has loaded, including all dependent resources(stylesheets, images).

title: What is the difference between native, host and user objects
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: Native objects are objects that are part of the JavaScript language defined by the ECMAScript specification. For example, String, Math, RegExp, Object, Function etc core objects defined in the ECMAScript spec. Host objects are objects provided by the browser or runtime environment (Node).

part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: Attributes are defined on the HTML markup whereas properties are defined on the DOM. For example, the below HTML element has 2 attributes: type and value.

title: What is same-origin policy
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: The same-origin policy is a policy that prevents JavaScript from making requests across domain boundaries. An origin is defined as a combination of URI scheme, hostname, and port number.

title: What is the purpose of void 0
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: Void(0) is used to prevent the page from refreshing. This will be helpful to eliminate the unwanted side-effect, because it will return the undefined primitive value. It is commonly used for HTML documents that use href="JavaScript:Void(0);" within an `` element.

title: Is JavaScript a compiled or interpreted language
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: JavaScript is an interpreted language, not a compiled language. An interpreter in the browser reads over the JavaScript code, interprets each line, and runs it. Nowadays modern browsers use a technology known as Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation, which compiles JavaScript to executable bytecode just as it is about to run.

title: Is JavaScript a case-sensitive language
part: Part 2: Promises, Callbacks, Async & Strict Mode (54 - 103)
summary: Yes, JavaScript is a case sensitive language. The language keywords, variables, function & object names, and any other identifiers must always be typed with a consistent capitalization of letters.

title: Is there any relation between Java and JavaScript
part: Part 3: DOM, Event Flow, Timers & Browser APIs (104 - 173)
summary: No, they are entirely two different programming languages and have nothing to do with each other. But both of them are Object Oriented Programming languages and like many other languages, they follow similar syntax for basic features(if, else, for, switch, break, continue etc).

title: What are events
part: Part 3: DOM, Event Flow, Timers & Browser APIs (104 - 173)
summary: Events are "things" that happen to HTML elements. When JavaScript is used in HTML pages, JavaScript can react on these events. Some of the examples of HTML events are: Web page has finished loading • Input field was changed • Button was clicked.

title: Who created javascript
part: Part 3: DOM, Event Flow, Timers & Browser APIs (104 - 173)
summary: JavaScript was created by Brendan Eich in 1995 during his time at Netscape Communications. Initially it was developed under the name Mocha, but later the language was officially called LiveScript when it first shipped in beta releases of Netscape.

title: What is the use of preventDefault method
part: Part 3: DOM, Event Flow, Timers & Browser APIs (104 - 173)
summary: The preventDefault() method cancels the event if it is cancelable, meaning that the default action or behaviour that belongs to the event will not occur. For example, prevent form submission when clicking on submit button and prevent opening the page URL when clicking on hyperlink are some common use cases.

title: What is the use of stopPropagation method
part: Part 3: DOM, Event Flow, Timers & Browser APIs (104 - 173)
summary: The stopPropagation method is used to stop the event from bubbling up the event chain. For example, the below nested divs with stopPropagation method prevents default event propagation when clicking on nested div(Div1).

title: What are the steps involved in return false usage
part: Part 3: DOM, Event Flow, Timers & Browser APIs (104 - 173)
summary: The return false statement in event handlers performs the below steps: First it stops the browser's default action or behaviour • It prevents the event from propagating the DOM • Stops callback execution and returns immediately when called.

title: What is BOM
part: Part 3: DOM, Event Flow, Timers & Browser APIs (104 - 173)
summary: The Browser Object Model (BOM) allows JavaScript to "talk to" the browser. It consists of the objects navigator, history, screen, location and document which are children of the window. The Browser Object Model is not standardized and can change based on different browsers.

title: What is the use of setTimeout
part: Part 3: DOM, Event Flow, Timers & Browser APIs (104 - 173)
summary: The setTimeout() method is used to call a function or evaluate an expression after a specified number of milliseconds. For example, let's log a message after 2 seconds using setTimeout method.

title: What is the use of setInterval
part: Part 3: DOM, Event Flow, Timers & Browser APIs (104 - 173)
summary: The setInterval() method is used to call a function or evaluate an expression at specified intervals (in milliseconds). For example, let's log a message after 2 seconds using setInterval method.

title: Why is JavaScript treated as Single threaded
part: Part 3: DOM, Event Flow, Timers & Browser APIs (104 - 173)
summary: JavaScript is a single-threaded language. Because the language specification does not allow the programmer to write code so that the interpreter can run parts of it in parallel in multiple threads or processes. Whereas languages like java, go, C++ can make multi-threaded and multi-process programs.

title: What is an event delegation
part: Part 3: DOM, Event Flow, Timers & Browser APIs (104 - 173)
summary: Event delegation is a technique where you attach one event listener to a parent element instead of adding listeners to each child element. It works because events bubble up from the target element to its parents.

title: What is ECMAScript
part: Part 3: DOM, Event Flow, Timers & Browser APIs (104 - 173)
summary: ECMAScript is the scripting language that forms the basis of JavaScript. ECMAScript standardized by the ECMA International standards organization in the ECMA-262 and ECMA-402 specifications. The first edition of ECMAScript was released in 1997.
