title: What are the SOLID Principles and why are they fundamental to software engineering?
part: Part 1: Core SOLID Principles & Fundamentals (1 - 10)
summary: SOLID is an acronym for 5 object-oriented design principles introduced by Robert C. Martin (Uncle Bob): S - Single Responsibility Principle (SRP): A class should have one, and only one, reason to change • O - Open/Closed Principle (OCP): Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification.

title: How do you implement the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) in practice?
part: Part 1: Core SOLID Principles & Fundamentals (1 - 10)
summary: A class should focus on a single concern: Violation: An Invoice class that calculates taxes, prints invoices to PDF, and saves invoices to a PostgreSQL database (3 reasons to change!) • Refactoring • Invoice: Manages line items and calculations • InvoicePdfGenerator: Handles PDF formatting.

title: How do you implement the Open/Closed Principle (OCP) using Polymorphism?
part: Part 1: Core SOLID Principles & Fundamentals (1 - 10)
summary: You should be able to add new functionality without modifying existing, tested source code: Violation: Using a massive switch(paymentType) statement inside processPayment() • Refactoring: Define a PaymentMethod interface; implement CreditCardPayment, PayPalPayment, and ApplePayPayment as independent classes.

title: What is the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) and what is the classic Rectangle-Square violation?
part: Part 1: Core SOLID Principles & Fundamentals (1 - 10)
summary: Subclasses must adhere to the behavioral contract of their parent class: The Rectangle-Square Violation • Square inherits from Rectangle • In Square, setting width automatically sets height to maintain a square • A function expecting a Rectangle sets width = 5 and height = 10 and expects area to be 50.

title: What is the Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)?
part: Part 1: Core SOLID Principles & Fundamentals (1 - 10)
summary: Many client-specific, granular interfaces are better than one bloated, "fat" interface: Violation: A monolithic Worker interface with work(), eat(), and sleep() • Refactoring: Split into Workable and Feedable interfaces.

title: What is the Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) and how does it differ from Dependency Injection (DI)?
part: Part 1: Core SOLID Principles & Fundamentals (1 - 10)
summary: Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP - The Design Principle): High-level business logic modules should not depend on low-level modules (e.g • Dependency Injection (DI - The Implementation Pattern): A technique where an object receives its dependencies from the outside (e.g. passed via.

title: What is High Cohesion and Low Coupling, and how do they balance software design?
part: Part 1: Core SOLID Principles & Fundamentals (1 - 10)
summary: High Cohesion: Elements within a module belong together and focus on performing one single, well-defined task • Low Coupling: Modules are loosely connected and independent; changes to one module do not ripple through or break other modules.

title: Why does Composition over Inheritance prevent the Fragile Base Class problem?
part: Part 1: Core SOLID Principles & Fundamentals (1 - 10)
summary: Inheritance is the tightest coupling in OOP because subclasses depend on the internal implementation details of the superclass. A change in the parent class can silently break subclass invariants (Fragile Base Class). Composition delegates behavior via interfaces, keeping boundaries clean and independently testable.

title: What is the Law of Demeter (Principle of Least Knowledge) and how do you spot train-wreck code?
part: Part 1: Core SOLID Principles & Fundamentals (1 - 10)
summary: A method should only call methods on: Itself (this) • Its parameters • Objects it instantiated directly • Its direct member fields.

title: Explain the Tell, Don't Ask principle and how it avoids Anemic Domain Models?
part: Part 1: Core SOLID Principles & Fundamentals (1 - 10)
summary: Rather than asking an object for its data, performing logic outside, and setting the data back (Ask), tell the object what to do and let it manipulate its own internal state, encapsulating business rules.

title: What is the DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) principle vs Accidental Duplication?
part: Part 2: Object-Oriented Design, Code Smells & Refactoring (11 - 24)
summary: DRY states: Every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous representation within a system.: Crucial Distinction: Code that looks identical but changes for different business reasons is Accidental Duplication.

title: What are YAGNI and KISS principles and how do they prevent over-engineering?
part: Part 2: Object-Oriented Design, Code Smells & Refactoring (11 - 24)
summary: YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It): Never write code or create abstractions based on speculation about future requirements • KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid): Systems work best when kept simple rather than complicated with unnecessary layers.

title: What is an Anemic Domain Model vs a Rich Domain Model?
part: Part 2: Object-Oriented Design, Code Smells & Refactoring (11 - 24)
summary: Anemic Domain Model: Classes contain only getters/setters with zero business logic (pure data bags); all business rules reside in procedural • Rich Domain Model: Domain entities encapsulate both data and business logic, defending their own invariants.

title: How do you defend Domain Invariants inside Domain Entities?
part: Part 2: Object-Oriented Design, Code Smells & Refactoring (11 - 24)
summary: A domain invariant is a business rule that must always be true throughout an entity's lifecycle. Protect invariants by: Making constructors private or validating all invariants upon creation • Eliminating public setters • Exposing intention-revealing methods that enforce validation.

title: What is Command Query Separation (CQS) at the class and method level?
part: Part 2: Object-Oriented Design, Code Smells & Refactoring (11 - 24)
summary: Every method should either be: A Command: Mutates system state, returns void • A Query: Returns a value, has zero side-effects on system state.

title: How do you identify the "God Object" Code Smell and how do you refactor it using SRP?
part: Part 2: Object-Oriented Design, Code Smells & Refactoring (11 - 24)
summary: A God Object knows too much or does too much (thousands of lines, dozens of dependencies). Refactor by grouping methods around distinct business actors and extracting cohesive single-purpose classes.

title: What is Primitive Obsession and how do Value Objects resolve it?
part: Part 2: Object-Oriented Design, Code Smells & Refactoring (11 - 24)
summary: Relying on raw primitives (string email, decimal amount) rather than domain models. A Value Object (EmailAddress, Money) encapsulates validation, formatting, and immutability.

title: What is Feature Envy and how do you resolve it?
part: Part 2: Object-Oriented Design, Code Smells & Refactoring (11 - 24)
summary: Occurs when a method in class A accesses getters of class B more than its own data. Resolve by moving the method into class B where the data naturally lives.

title: How do you design for Testability using the Dependency Inversion Principle?
part: Part 2: Object-Oriented Design, Code Smells & Refactoring (11 - 24)
summary: High-level classes depend on interface abstractions injected via constructors. In unit tests, inject test doubles (mocks/stubs) without spinning up databases, file systems, or network sockets.

title: What is Interface Pollution and how does the Interface Segregation Principle prevent it?
part: Part 2: Object-Oriented Design, Code Smells & Refactoring (11 - 24)
summary: Occurs when an interface accumulates dozens of unrelated methods. Clients are forced to implement dummy methods they never use. Segregate into smaller, role-focused interfaces (Readable, Writable, Closeable).

title: How does the Liskov Substitution Principle apply to Exception Contracts?
part: Part 2: Object-Oriented Design, Code Smells & Refactoring (11 - 24)
summary: Subclasses cannot throw broader checked exceptions than their superclasses. A subclass method must honor the exception contract of the base abstraction to prevent unexpected crashes.

title: What are Preconditions and Postconditions in Design by Contract (LSP)?
part: Part 2: Object-Oriented Design, Code Smells & Refactoring (11 - 24)
summary: Preconditions: Cannot be strengthened in a subtype (cannot demand stricter inputs) • Postconditions: Cannot be weakened in a subtype (cannot guarantee less outputs).

title: What is Shotgun Surgery vs Divergent Change?
part: Part 2: Object-Oriented Design, Code Smells & Refactoring (11 - 24)
summary: Divergent Change: A single class is modified for multiple unrelated reasons (violates SRP) • Shotgun Surgery: A single business change forces dozens of edits across many different classes.

title: How do you refactor Legacy Code toward SOLID using Automated Characterization Tests?
part: Part 2: Object-Oriented Design, Code Smells & Refactoring (11 - 24)
summary: Before refactoring legacy code with zero tests, write Characterization Tests that capture the current actual behavior of the system (bugs and all) to provide a safety net.

title: How do SOLID principles apply at the Microservices boundary level?
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: SRP: A service owns a single business capability • OCP: Extend service features via event listeners rather than modifying existing APIs • DIP: Services communicate via standardized API schemas and contracts.

title: Explain the Common Closure Principle (CCP) and Common Reuse Principle (CRP)?
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: CCP: Classes that change together should be packaged together in the same module • CRP: Classes that are not used together should not be packaged together.

title: What is the Acyclic Dependencies Principle (ADP) in enterprise package architecture?
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: The dependency graph of packages must contain no cycles (no mutual A -> B -> A dependencies). Break cycles by applying DIP and introducing an interface.

title: What is the Stable Abstractions Principle (SAP) and Stable Dependencies Principle (SDP)?
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: SDP: Depend in the direction of stability (depend on modules that are harder to change) • SAP: A stable module should also be abstract (interfaces/abstract classes) so it can be extended.

title: How do you enforce SOLID and Architectural Rules in CI/CD using ArchUnit or NetArchTest?
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: Write automated architectural fitness tests that fail in CI/CD if developers violate SOLID rules (e.g. domain layer depending on infrastructure, or circular package dependencies).

title: How do you apply SOLID in Functional and Modern Multi-Paradigm Languages (TypeScript, Go, Rust)?
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: In languages without classic class inheritance, SOLID is applied via function composition, traits (Rust), implicit interfaces (Go), and structural typing (TypeScript).

title: What is the Rule of Three in software refactoring and avoiding Premature Abstraction?
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: Don't extract a shared abstraction when you see code duplicated once. Wait until you write it for the third time so you have enough data points to create the correct abstraction.

title: How does Encapsulation differ from Information Hiding?
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: Encapsulation: Bundling data with methods that operate on that data • Information Hiding: Concealing design decisions and data structures behind stable interfaces to protect clients from change.

title: What is Static vs Dynamic Polymorphism and what are their performance trade-offs?
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: Dynamic Polymorphism: Virtual method dispatch via v-tables at runtime; flexible but adds pointer indirection • Static Polymorphism: Generics and templates resolved at compile-time; zero runtime overhead and can be inlined.

title: How do you refactor an enterprise Payment Processing system adhering to all 5 SOLID principles?
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: SRP: Separate payment validation, gateway API calls, and invoice generation into distinct classes • OCP: Add new payment gateways (Stripe, PayPal, Crypto) by implementing PaymentGateway interface without modifying existing checkout code • LSP: Ensure all gateways return standardized result types and honor timeout contracts.

title: When does strict adherence to SOLID harm software development velocity and performance?
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: Blindly creating 5 interfaces and factories for simple CRUD operations creates excessive indirection and mental fatigue. Balance SOLID with pragmatism: apply principles where business logic actually changes.

title: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) and the "Reason to Change": Actor-driven responsibilities.
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: Robert C. Martin ("Uncle Bob") refined SRP: "A module should be responsible to one, and only one, actor (stakeholder/user group)": The Violation Example: An Employee class containing calculatePay() (owned by CFO/Finance), reportHours() (owned by COO/Operations), and save().

title: Open/Closed Principle (OCP) via Strategy and Plugin Architectures.
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: "Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification": When adding a new shipping carrier (DHL) to an e-commerce platform, you should never open and edit existing shipping calculation code with a new • Plugin / Strategy Architecture.

title: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) Contracts: Preconditions, Postconditions, and Invariants.
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: Formulated by Barbara Liskov: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering program correctness.: Preconditions cannot be strengthened: If base method process(amount) accepts any positive number (> 0), a subclass cannot demand amount >= 100.

title: Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) vs Fat Interfaces.
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: "Clients should not be forced to depend upon interfaces that they do not use": Fat Interface Anti-Pattern: An AllInOnePrinter interface declaring print(), scan(), fax(), and staple() • Role Interfaces: Split into lean, granular capabilities • Printer { print() } • Scanner { scan() }.

title: Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) vs Inversion of Control (IoC) vs Dependency Injection (DI).
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: Clarifying the three frequently confused terms: DIP (Architectural Principle): High-level business logic modules must not depend on low-level implementation modules (databases, APIs) • IoC (Design Pattern / Concept): Inverting the traditional control flow.

title: SOLID in Microservices Architecture.
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: Applying object-oriented principles to distributed systems: SRP in Microservices: Each microservice owns a single business capability and one bounded context database • OCP via Event-Driven Architecture: An Order Service emits an OrderPlaced event to Kafka.

title: SOLID in Functional Programming.
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: How SOLID manifests in functional languages (Clojure, Haskell, Elixir, Scala): SRP: Pure functions that do exactly one thing: accept input, return output, zero side effects • OCP: Higher-order functions • LSP: Strong algebraic type systems where sum types and pattern matching guarantee exhaustiveness.

title: Refactoring God Classes to SRP: Facades and Delegation.
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: Refactoring a 5,000-line monolithic UserManager class: Identify cohesive clusters of methods • Auth & Passwords -> Extract to AuthenticationService • Email Notifications -> Extract to UserEmailNotifier • Profile Billing -> Extract to UserSubscriptionService.

title: The Circle-Ellipse and Square-Rectangle Dilemma in LSP.
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: In mathematics, a Square is a special type of Rectangle (width = height). In Object-Oriented Programming, modeling Square extends Rectangle violates LSP.

title: Interface Pollution and YAGNI: Detecting premature abstraction.
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: Interface Pollution Anti-Pattern: Creating an IUserService interface for every single UserService when there is only ever one concrete • Creates indirection, requires clicking through two files in IDEs, and provides zero business value.

title: DIP in Clean Architecture / Hexagonal Architecture (Ports and Adapters).
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: The Core Invariant: The domain layer (Entities and Use Cases) sits at the center and knows nothing about databases, web frameworks, or • Ports (Interfaces): Defined inside the Domain layer (e.g. UserRepository, EmailSender).

title: Testing Benefits of SOLID.
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: Fast Unit Tests: When classes follow SRP, they have few dependencies, allowing unit tests to run in microseconds without booting heavy • Trivial Mocking via DIP: Because dependencies are injected as interfaces, test suites can pass in-memory fake repositories or mock gateways instantly.

title: Anti-Patterns Violating SOLID: Shotgun Surgery vs Divergent Change.
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: Divergent Change (Violates SRP): When one class has to be modified in different ways every time different business requirements change (e.g • Shotgun Surgery (Opposite of SRP): When a single business change requires making dozens of small edits scattered across 15 different classes.

title: SOLID and Concurrency: Thread safety invariants and immutable value objects.
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: In multi-threaded environments, mutable state violates class invariants under concurrent access: Immutable Value Objects: Making domain entities immutable (e.g. record in Java/C#, frozen objects in TypeScript) guarantees that class state can.

title: Pragmatic Architecture: Balancing SOLID with KISS and YAGNI.
part: Part 3: Enterprise Architecture, Package Design & Enforcement (25 - 35)
summary: Architecture is about trade-offs, not dogma: KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid): Favor simple, readable code over clever abstractions • YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It): Do not build generalized abstract plugin architectures for features that might never be built • The Pragmatic Guideline: Start with simple, cohesive procedural code.

title: What are the three Gang of Four (GoF) Pattern Categories?
part: Part 1: Creational & Structural Patterns (1 - 10)
summary: Creational Patterns: Deal with object creation mechanisms, increasing flexibility and reuse of existing code (Factory, Builder, Singleton, Prototype) • Structural Patterns: Explain how to assemble objects and classes into larger structures while keeping them flexible and efficient (Adapter.

title: What is the Singleton Pattern and how do you implement it thread-safely?
part: Part 1: Creational & Structural Patterns (1 - 10)
summary: Ensures a class has only one instance and provides a global access point to it: Private constructor prevents direct instantiation • Static instance variable and public static getter • Double-Checked Locking (in Java / C#).

title: What is the Factory Method Pattern?
part: Part 1: Creational & Structural Patterns (1 - 10)
summary: Defines an interface for creating an object, but lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate: Decouples client code from concrete implementation classes.

title: What is the Builder Pattern and when should you use it?
part: Part 1: Creational & Structural Patterns (1 - 10)
summary: Separates the construction of a complex object from its representation, allowing the same construction process to create different representations: Use Case: Eliminates "Telescoping Constructors" where a class constructor has 10 parameters, most of which are optional.

title: What is the Adapter Pattern and how does it reconcile incompatible interfaces?
part: Part 1: Creational & Structural Patterns (1 - 10)
summary: Acts as a translator / wrapper between two incompatible interfaces: Analogy: A US-to-European power plug adapter • Example: Your legacy application expects an interface LegacyPaymentGateway.charge(cents), but a new third-party SDK provides.

title: What is the Decorator Pattern and how does it differ from Inheritance?
part: Part 1: Creational & Structural Patterns (1 - 10)
summary: Attaches new behaviors to objects dynamically at runtime by placing them inside special wrapper objects: Inheritance: Static (compile-time) and causes class explosion (e.g. EspressoWithMilk, EspressoWithMilkAndCaramel) • Decorator: You wrap a base object with multiple decorators dynamically.

title: What is the Facade Pattern and how does it simplify complex subsystems?
part: Part 1: Creational & Structural Patterns (1 - 10)
summary: Provides a simple, unified, high-level interface to a complex library, framework, or set of classes: Analogy: A customer service representative who handles your order, billing, and shipping behind the scenes • Instead of client code orchestrating 10 classes (AudioCodec, VideoBuffer, HardwareDecoder, ColorCorrection), you provide a simple.

title: What is the Proxy Pattern and what are its common types (Virtual, Protection, Remote)?
part: Part 1: Creational & Structural Patterns (1 - 10)
summary: Provides a surrogate or placeholder object that controls access to the real object: Virtual Proxy (Lazy Loading): Defers the creation of an expensive object (e.g. a 50 MB high-resolution image) until it is actually requested.

title: What is the Strategy Pattern and how does it eliminate `if/else` ladders?
part: Part 1: Creational & Structural Patterns (1 - 10)
summary: Defines a family of interchangeable algorithms, encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable at runtime: Context: Holds a reference to a Strategy interface • Client passes the desired strategy dynamically.

title: What is the Observer Pattern and how does it implement Pub/Sub?
part: Part 1: Creational & Structural Patterns (1 - 10)
summary: Defines a one-to-many dependency between objects so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified and updated automatically: Subject: Maintains a list of observers; provides subscribe() and unsubscribe() • Observer: Defines an update() method called by the Subject.

title: What is the Command Pattern and how does it enable Undo / Redo?
part: Part 2: Behavioral Patterns & Communication (11 - 24)
summary: Encapsulates a request as an object, thereby letting you parameterize clients with different requests, queue or log requests, and support reversible operations: Every command object implements execute() and undo() • An Invoker maintains a history stack • Running a command: Calls cmd.execute() and pushes to stack.

title: What is the State Pattern and how does it differ from the Strategy Pattern?
part: Part 2: Behavioral Patterns & Communication (11 - 24)
summary: Allows an object to alter its behavior when its internal state changes, appearing as if the object changed its class: Strategy vs State • Strategy: Client explicitly chooses which algorithm strategy to inject; strategies rarely know about other strategies.

title: What is the Template Method Pattern?
part: Part 2: Behavioral Patterns & Communication (11 - 24)
summary: Defines the skeleton of an algorithm in an abstract base class, deferring some steps to subclasses without changing the algorithm's overall structure: Uses invariant steps and abstract hooks.

title: What is the Chain of Responsibility Pattern?
part: Part 2: Behavioral Patterns & Communication (11 - 24)
summary: Passes a request along a dynamic chain of handlers: Upon receiving a request, each handler decides either to process the request or to pass it to the next handler in the chain • The standard pattern behind HTTP Middleware pipelines (Express, Koa, ASP.NET Core) and authentication filters.

title: What is Clean Architecture (The Onion / Hexagonal Architecture)?
part: Part 2: Behavioral Patterns & Communication (11 - 24)
summary: Introduced by Uncle Bob to create systems independent of frameworks, databases, and UI: Dependency Rule: Dependencies always point inwards toward the core domain! • Entities (Core Domain): Pure business rules and models (Zero external dependencies) • Use Cases (Application Business Rules): Orchestrates data flow to/from entities.

title: What is Hexagonal Architecture (Ports and Adapters)?
part: Part 2: Behavioral Patterns & Communication (11 - 24)
summary: Created by Alistair Cockburn: The core application resides inside a hexagon, isolated from the outside world • Ports: Inward-facing application interfaces (e.g. OrderRepositoryPort, PaymentProcessorPort) • Adapters: Outward-facing concrete implementations that plug into ports.

title: What is the Repository Pattern and what are its benefits?
part: Part 2: Behavioral Patterns & Communication (11 - 24)
summary: Mediates between the domain and data mapping layers, acting like an in-memory collection of domain objects: Encapsulates database query logic (SELECT, INSERT) behind a collection-like interface (findById, save, delete) • Decouples domain logic from ORMs (Prisma, TypeORM, Hibernate) and SQL dialects.

title: What is the Unit of Work Pattern?
part: Part 2: Behavioral Patterns & Communication (11 - 24)
summary: Instead of saving every entity modification to the database immediately (incurring 10 separate SQL round-trips) • The Unit of Work tracks all dirty, new, and deleted objects in memory, and commits them inside a single atomic database transaction upon completion.

title: What is the CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) Pattern?
part: Part 2: Behavioral Patterns & Communication (11 - 24)
summary: Segregates the data model for write operations (Commands) from the data model for read operations (Queries): Command Model: Optimized strictly for validating business rules, transactions, and maintaining invariants (writes to normalized relational DB).

title: What is the Event Sourcing Pattern?
part: Part 2: Behavioral Patterns & Communication (11 - 24)
summary: Instead of storing only the current state of an entity, Event Sourcing stores the entire append-only sequence of immutable domain events that led to that state: Bank Account Balance is not stored as 500 • Instead, the database stores • AccountCreated (+0) • MoneyDeposited (+$1000).

title: What is the Outbox Pattern and how does it guarantee Dual-Write consistency?
part: Part 2: Behavioral Patterns & Communication (11 - 24)
summary: When an app must update a database AND publish an event to a message broker (Kafka/RabbitMQ): The Dual-Write Problem: If the database commit succeeds but the network fails before publishing to Kafka, data is out-of-sync! • Transactional Outbox Pattern.

title: What is the SAGA Pattern for Distributed Transactions?
part: Part 2: Behavioral Patterns & Communication (11 - 24)
summary: Replaces slow 2-Phase Commit (2PC) across microservices with a sequence of local transactions: Each service executes a local transaction and publishes an event that triggers the next service's transaction.

title: What is the Circuit Breaker Pattern in distributed systems?
part: Part 2: Behavioral Patterns & Communication (11 - 24)
summary: Prevents cascading failures when a downstream microservice is down: Closed State: Normal operation; requests pass through • Open State: When failure rate exceeds a threshold (e.g. 50% timeouts), the circuit opens immediately • Half-Open State: After a timeout, sends a single test probe request.

title: What is the Bulkhead Pattern?
part: Part 2: Behavioral Patterns & Communication (11 - 24)
summary: Inspired by nautical ship bulkheads that compartmentalize hulls so a leak in one compartment doesn't sink the entire ship: Isolates critical resources into independent pools (thread pools, connection pools, CPU allocations) • Example: Allocate 30 threads for standard customer checkout, and 5 threads for third-party analytics.

title: What is the Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL) in Domain-Driven Design?
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: A translation layer placed between a modern domain model and a legacy system or third-party service: Translates legacy data models and terminology into clean domain objects before they enter your domain core • Prevents legacy system bad practices and archaic concepts from "corrupting" your modern domain design.

title: What is the difference between Anemic Domain Model and Rich Domain Model?
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: Anemic Domain Model (Anti-Pattern): Entities are purely dumb data holders with public getters/setters (class Order { public items, status; }) • Rich Domain Model (Best Practice): Entities encapsulate both data and the business logic that operates on that data (order.cancel(), order.addItem()).

title: What is the Strangler Fig Pattern for monolithic migration?
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: A pattern to incrementally migrate a legacy monolithic application to microservices without a risky "Big Bang" rewrite: Place an API Gateway in front of the monolith • Implement new features or carve out individual capabilities (e.g. Authentication) as new microservices.

title: What is the Sidecar Pattern in Cloud-Native architectures?
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: Deploys components of an application into a separate process or container to provide supporting features without modifying the primary application code: Common examples in Kubernetes Pods • Envoy Proxy sidecar (Service Mesh for mTLS, traffic routing, metrics) • Fluentd / Datadog sidecar (Log harvesting).

title: When does Design Pattern Over-Engineering harm software projects?
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: Applying GoF patterns blindly where simple procedural code is sufficient ("Patternitis"): Introducing 5 layers of Factories, Builders, and Adapters for a CRUD service that will only ever query a single PostgreSQL table • Increases cognitive load, makes debugging painful, and inflates codebase size.

title: What is the Abstract Factory Pattern and how does it differ from Factory Method?
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: Factory Method: Uses inheritance to delegate creation of a single product to subclasses • Abstract Factory: Uses object composition to create families of related or dependent products (e.g., MacButton + MacCheckbox vs WinButton +.

title: What is the Prototype Pattern and when should you use Cloning over constructors?
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: The Prototype Pattern creates new objects by copying (cloning) an existing instance rather than constructing from scratch.: Use Case: When object creation is computationally expensive (e.g. database loading, network lookups, complex calculations).

title: What is the Composite Pattern and how does it treat trees of objects uniformly?
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: The Composite Pattern organizes objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies. Clients treat individual leaf objects (e.g., File) and composite containers (e.g., Directory) through a single unified interface.

title: What is the Bridge Pattern and how does it prevent a Cartesian explosion of subclasses?
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: The Bridge Pattern decouples an abstraction from its implementation so that both can vary independently. Instead of multiplying classes (M views \times N platforms = M \times N classes), the abstraction holds a reference to an implementation interface (M + N classes).

title: What is the Flyweight Pattern and how does it minimize memory by sharing intrinsic state?
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: The Flyweight Pattern shares common, immutable data (Intrinsic State) across millions of objects rather than duplicating it in every instance. Mutable, context-specific data (Extrinsic State) is passed in dynamically.

title: What is the Visitor Pattern and how does it add new operations without modifying existing classes?
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: The Visitor Pattern uses Double Dispatch (element.accept(visitor) -> visitor.visit(element)) to separate an algorithm from the object structure on which it operates, allowing new operations to be added without modifying the element classes.

title: Chain of Responsibility Pattern: Middleware pipelines and event bubbling.
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: Avoids coupling the sender of a request to its receiver by giving multiple objects a chance to handle the request: Handlers are chained together sequentially • Real-World Examples.

title: State Pattern vs Strategy Pattern: Structural similarities and behavioral differences.
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: Both patterns look structurally identical (a Context class delegating to an interface): Strategy Pattern: The client configures the Context with a specific algorithm (e.g. FastRouteStrategy vs ScenicRouteStrategy).

title: Mediator Pattern: Decoupling communication dependencies into a central hub.
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: When dozens of components communicate directly with each other, they form a chaotic O(N^2) web of tight coupling: Mediator Pattern: Components (Colleagues) communicate strictly through a central Mediator object • Real-World Example.

title: Memento Pattern: Snapshotting internal state for undo/redo workflows.
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: Captures and externalizes an object's internal state so the object can be restored to this state later, without violating encapsulation: Originator: The business object (e.g. Text Editor canvas) • Memento: Immutable state snapshot container.

title: Interpreter Pattern: Building Domain-Specific Languages (DSLs) and rule engines.
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: Given a language, defines a representation for its grammar along with an interpreter that evaluates sentences in the language: Represents grammar rules as an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) composed of Terminal Expressions (literal numbers, variable names) and Non-Terminal.

title: Service Locator Anti-Pattern vs Dependency Injection.
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: Service Locator: A central registry object that classes query to fetch dependencies.

title: Saga Pattern (Choreography vs Orchestration): Distributed transactions.
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: In a microservices architecture, you cannot use distributed ACID database locks (2PC) across services without catastrophic latency. A Saga is a sequence of local transactions: If Step 3 (Payment) fails, the Saga executes Compensating Transactions in reverse order (e.g. cancel reserved inventory, cancel pending order).

title: Strangler Fig Pattern: Incrementally modernizing legacy monolithic systems.
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: Named after strangler fig trees that grow around host trees and gradually replace them: Instead of attempting a high-risk "Big Bang" rewrite of a 10-year-old monolith • Place an API Gateway / Reverse Proxy in front of the monolith • Implement new features or extract single domains (e.g. /billing) as modern microservices.

title: Bulkhead Pattern: Isolating critical resources to prevent total system collapse.
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: Derived from naval ship hulls that divide the ship into watertight compartments (bulkheads): if water leaks into one section, the ship stays afloat: In software, partition resources (thread pools, connection pools, memory) • Dedicate 50 threads to the core Checkout service • Dedicate 10 threads to the third-party Recommendation service.

title: Ambassador Pattern: Offloading client-side connectivity to a local proxy.
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: Deploys a helper service alongside a client application (typically as a localhost process or Kubernetes sidecar): The application connects to localhost:8080 using standard plaintext HTTP • The Ambassador Proxy handles • Routing to remote cloud services • mTLS certificate encryption.

title: Sharding / Partitioning Pattern: Horizontal data scaling.
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: When a single database server hits physical CPU or disk capacity limits: Split the dataset horizontally across multiple distinct database servers (Shards) • Range-Based Sharding: Shard 1 holds IDs 1 - 1,000,000; Shard 2 holds 1,000,001 - 2,000,000 • Hash-Based Sharding: hash(customerid) % numshards.

title: Gateway Aggregation / Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) Pattern.
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: Gateway Aggregation: An API Gateway aggregates multiple backend microservice calls into a single HTTP round-trip, saving cellular network • Backend-for-Frontend (BFF): Instead of a single monolithic API Gateway serving all clients, create dedicated gateway layers tailored to specific.

title: Competing Consumers Pattern: Scalable concurrent message processing.
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: When the message production rate exceeds the processing capacity of a single consumer: Multiple identical consumer instances attach to a single shared message queue (RabbitMQ queue, AWS SQS) • The message broker dispenses each message to strictly one consumer in the pool.

title: Claim Check Pattern: Handling large message payloads in event-driven systems.
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: Message brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS) are designed for small payloads (< 256 KB); sending 50MB PDF files or 4K videos directly through message queues degrades broker memory and throughput: Claim Check Workflow • Producer uploads the 50MB file directly to cloud object storage (AWS S3 / GCS).

title: Architectural Anti-Patterns: Golden Hammer, Lava Flow, and Big Ball of Mud.
part: Part 3: Architectural Patterns & Enterprise Systems (25 - 35)
summary: Recognizing toxic architectural anti-patterns: Golden Hammer: Assuming a single favorite technology (e.g. Microservices, GraphQL, or MongoDB) is the universal solution for every single problem.

title: What is Domain-Driven Design (DDD) and what problem does it solve?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational Concepts (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: Domain-Driven Design (introduced by Eric Evans) is an approach to software development that centers the entire system design around a deep, evolving model of the core business problem (The Domain): Problem It Solves: In large enterprise software, complexity is usually not in the technical framework (React, Spring, Docker); it is in the.

title: What is the difference between Strategic DDD and Tactical DDD?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational Concepts (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: Strategic DDD (The Big Picture - High-Level Architecture): Focuses on decomposing a large complex enterprise into clear subsystems • Ubiquitous Language, Bounded Contexts, Subdomains (Core, Supporting, Generic), and Context Maps • Determines microservice boundaries and team ownership.

title: What is the Ubiquitous Language and why is it essential?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational Concepts (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: A single, unambiguous, shared vocabulary created jointly by software developers and business domain experts: Rule: The exact same terminology used in business discussions must be used verbatim in requirements docs, user stories, class names, method.

title: What is a Bounded Context?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational Concepts (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: A linguistic and conceptual boundary within which a specific domain model and Ubiquitous Language applies strictly and consistently: In an enterprise e-commerce system, the word "Product" means completely different things to different teams • In Sales Context: A Product has a price, marketing copy, and photos.

title: What are the three types of Subdomains (Core, Supporting, Generic)?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational Concepts (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: Core Domain: The primary competitive advantage of your business • Supporting Subdomain: Complements the core business • Generic Subdomain: Universal business problems with zero competitive differentiation (e.g. Billing, Identity/Auth, Invoicing).

title: What is the difference between an Entity and a Value Object?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational Concepts (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: The most fundamental distinction in Tactical DDD: Entity: Defined by its persistent Identity (ID), not by its attributes • Value Object: Defined entirely by the combination of its attributes, with NO identity • Example: Money(amount: 50, currency: "USD") or Address(street, zip).

title: What is an Aggregate and an Aggregate Root?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational Concepts (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: Aggregate: A cluster of associated domain objects (Entities and Value Objects) treated as a single unit for data changes and transactional • Example: An Order (Aggregate Root) containing multiple OrderItem entities and a ShippingAddress value object.

title: What is a Domain Invariant?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational Concepts (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: A business rule that must be true at all times within an Aggregate's lifecycle: Examples • "The total cost of an Order cannot exceed the customer's credit limit." • "An order cannot have more than 50 items." • "A shipment cannot be created without at least one item.".

title: What is a Domain Service and when should you use it?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational Concepts (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: A stateless service that encapsulates business domain logic that naturally does not belong to any single Entity or Value Object: Use Case: Operations that involve multiple aggregates or external calculations (e.g. FundsTransferService.transfer(fromAccount, toAccount, amount)).

title: What is an Anemic Domain Model and why is it considered an Anti-Pattern?
part: Part 1: Basic & Foundational Concepts (Junior / Entry-Level)
summary: An anemic model is where domain classes are just dumb property bags with public getters and setters (get/set), containing zero business logic: All validation, calculations, and invariants are pushed into bloated procedural service classes (OrderService).

title: What is a Domain Event and how does it represent business facts?
part: Part 2: Core Architecture & Implementation (Mid-Level)
summary: A record of something meaningful that has already happened in the domain in the past: Characteristics: Immutable, named in the past tense (OrderPlaced, PaymentReceived, UserRegistered) • Captures the exact point-in-time snapshot of the state change.

title: What is the difference between Domain Events, Integration Events, and Application Events?
part: Part 2: Core Architecture & Implementation (Mid-Level)
summary: Domain Event: Internal to a single Bounded Context • Integration Event: Published externally across network boundaries (via Kafka, RabbitMQ, EventBridge) to notify other Bounded Contexts (e.g • Application Event: Framework-level events (e.g. user logged in, HTTP request started, cache cleared).

title: What is the difference between Domain Services, Application Services, and Infrastructure Services?
part: Part 2: Core Architecture & Implementation (Mid-Level)
summary: Three distinct service layers in DDD architectures: Domain Service: Pure business logic that spans multiple aggregates (e.g. PricingEngineService) • Application Service: Orchestration layer (Use Cases).

title: What are Context Maps and the standard Context Relationships?
part: Part 2: Core Architecture & Implementation (Mid-Level)
summary: A Context Map visualizes the structural and political relationships between different Bounded Contexts in an enterprise: Shared Kernel: Two contexts share a common core domain model and database subset (requires tight coordination) • Customer / Supplier (Upstream / Downstream - U/D): Upstream (U) provides data; Downstream (D) consumes it.

title: How does the Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL) protect domain models?
part: Part 2: Core Architecture & Implementation (Mid-Level)
summary: When integrating with an external vendor or legacy system: Never let external terminology and bad data structures leak into your domain! • The ACL acts as a bidirectional translator • Takes raw external JSON/XML, parses it, validates it, and maps it into clean, strongly typed internal Domain Entities and Value Objects.

title: What is the Repository Pattern in DDD and what is its strict contract?
part: Part 2: Core Architecture & Implementation (Mid-Level)
summary: A Repository simulates an in-memory collection of Aggregate Roots: Rule 1: Only Aggregate Roots can have Repositories! • Rule 2: The repository interface lives in the Domain Layer, but its implementation lives in the Infrastructure Layer (DIP).

title: How should Aggregate boundaries be sized?
part: Part 2: Core Architecture & Implementation (Mid-Level)
summary: The #1 beginner mistake in DDD is creating massive, bloated aggregates (e.g. a Customer aggregate containing all historical orders, invoices, reviews, and tickets): Large aggregates cause severe database locking contention, high memory consumption, and transaction deadlocks! • Best Practice (Small Aggregates).

title: What is the difference between Immediate Consistency and Eventual Consistency in DDD?
part: Part 2: Core Architecture & Implementation (Mid-Level)
summary: Immediate (Strong) Consistency: Enforced strictly within the boundary of a single Aggregate using database ACID transactions • Eventual Consistency: Used across multiple Aggregates or across Bounded Contexts • When Aggregate A changes, it publishes a Domain Event • A background handler updates Aggregate B moments later.

title: How do Factories work in Domain-Driven Design?
part: Part 2: Core Architecture & Implementation (Mid-Level)
summary: When creating an Aggregate Root requires complex validation, default invariants, or assembly of nested value objects: Encapsulate the creation logic inside a dedicated Factory (method or class) • Guarantees that an entity can never exist in an invalid, half-initialized state.

title: What is Event Storming and how does it discover Bounded Contexts?
part: Part 2: Core Architecture & Implementation (Mid-Level)
summary: A rapid, collaborative workshop method that brings together developers and business domain experts around a large paper roll: Orange Sticky Notes (Domain Events): Participants write down all business events in past tense ("Order Placed", "Invoice Generated") • Blue Notes (Commands): What triggered the event?

title: How do you implement the Outbox Pattern with Domain Events in production?
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: To ensure Domain Events are never lost if the message broker is unreachable: When saving an Aggregate, the Repository extracts all uncommitted domain events recorded by the aggregate • In the same atomic database transaction, it writes the aggregate row AND inserts the events into an outbox table.

title: What is the SAGA Pattern (Choreography vs Orchestration) in DDD microservices?
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: Manages distributed business transactions across multiple Bounded Contexts without 2PC: Choreography: Event-driven • OrderService emits OrderCreated -> PaymentService listens and charges card -> emits PaymentCompleted -> InventoryService reserves stock • Simple for small workflows; difficult to track and debug as services scale.

title: What are Compensating Transactions in Sagas?
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: Because distributed transactions cannot execute a database ROLLBACK across independent microservices, Sagas use compensating actions: A compensating transaction is an explicit business operation that semantically reverses a prior committed action • Original action: CreditCardCharged (100) -> Compensating action: RefundIssued (100).

title: What is CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) in DDD?
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: Splits the application into two independent models: Write Side (Commands): Uses Tactical DDD • Read Side (Queries): Bypasses domain aggregates and repositories completely! • Allows scaling read performance independently (e.g. 100,000 queries/sec on read replicas) without burdening transactional write aggregates.

title: What is Event Sourcing and how does it integrate with DDD Aggregates?
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: In an Event-Sourced aggregate, the state of the entity is reconstructed dynamically by replaying its domain events: The database stores an events stream table: (aggregateid, version, eventtype, payload) • When loading an aggregate • Fetch all events where aggregate_id = 'ORD-101' ordered by version • Instantiate an empty Order object.

title: How do you model Complex Business Rules using the Specification Pattern?
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: Encapsulates a business rule or validation predicate into an independent, reusable boolean specification object: Allows chaining specifications using boolean logic (and, or, not).

title: How do you handle Concurrency and Race Conditions on Aggregate Roots?
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: Use Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC): Store a version integer on the Aggregate Root • When committing updates via the repository • If another concurrent request already updated the aggregate (version is already 4), the update affects 0 rows.

title: What is the Open Host Service (OHS) and Published Language (PL)?
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: When an Upstream Bounded Context must serve multiple Downstream consumer teams: Instead of building custom custom integrations for each client • Open Host Service (OHS): Upstream exposes a stable, documented public subsystem (REST API, gRPC service).

title: What is the Separate Ways pattern in Strategic DDD?
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: When the coordination, political overhead, and network integration cost between two teams exceeds the benefit of software integration: Both teams deliberately choose to go their separate ways and build independent solutions tailored to their specific needs.

title: How do you model Temporal / Time-Series data in DDD?
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: Time is an explicit first-class citizen in business domains: Never store just a mutable status without context • Use explicit Date Range Value Objects: DateRange(start: Date, end: Date) with intersection and overlap methods (rangeA.overlaps(rangeB)).

title: What is the Customer / Supplier relationship in Context Mapping?
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: An Upstream (Supplier) / Downstream (Customer) relationship where the Upstream team's priorities are directly driven by Downstream needs: Downstream team submits feature requests and requirements • Upstream team plans and prioritizes their sprint backlogs to satisfy Downstream deliverables.

title: How do you implement Idempotency in Domain Event Consumers?
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: Message brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ) provide at-least-once delivery, meaning event handlers will occasionally receive the exact same event multiple times: Idempotent Consumer Pattern • Consumer inspects incoming eventId (UUID) • Queries a local processed_events database table • If eventId exists -> Acknowledge and discard immediately!.

title: What is the difference between Domain Exceptions and Technical Exceptions?
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: Technical Exceptions: Unexpected infrastructure failures (network timeout, database connection dropped, disk full) • Domain Exceptions: Expected business invariant violations (e.g. InsufficientFundsException, ProductOutOfStockException, OrderAlreadyShippedException).

title: How do you prevent Microservices from becoming a "Distributed Monolith" using DDD?
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: A distributed monolith happens when microservices are cut along technical layers (UI service, Logic service, Database service) or share database tables: DDD Solution • Cut microservices strictly along Bounded Context boundaries • Shared Nothing: Each microservice owns its private database.

title: When is Domain-Driven Design (DDD) an Anti-Pattern?
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: Applying full Tactical DDD to simple software: Simple CRUD applications: If an app simply reads and writes forms to database tables with minimal business rules, applying Aggregates • Short-lived throwaway prototypes / MVPs: Focus on product-market fit first before investing in deep domain models.

title: Ubiquitous Language in Practice: Resolving linguistic ambiguity across departments.
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: In large enterprises, different departments use the same word with completely different meanings: To Sales, an Account is a sales prospect with a budget and contract negotiations • To Engineering / Security, an Account is a login username, password hash, and permission roles.

title: Subdomains Classification: Core Domain vs Supporting vs Generic Subdomains.
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: Prioritizing engineering talent and budget: Core Domain: The unique secret sauce that provides competitive advantage and differentiates your business from competitors (e.g., Netflix.

title: Event Storming Workshop Methodology: Rapid domain discovery.
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: A collaborative, rapid modeling workshop uniting domain business experts with software engineers using colored sticky notes: Domain Events (Orange Sticky Notes): Written in past tense (OrderPlaced, InvoicePaid, AccountSuspended) arranged chronologically on a wall.

title: Context Mapping Patterns: Relationships between Bounded Contexts.
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: How different teams and systems integrate across context boundaries: Shared Kernel: Two teams share a small common subset of code and database tables • Partnership: Two teams succeed or fail together; features are planned jointly • Customer-Supplier: Upstream (Supplier) builds what Downstream (Customer) requires.

title: The 4 Aggregate Design Rules by Vaughn Vernon.
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: Essential guidelines for high-performance, maintainable Aggregates: Rule 1: Model True Business Invariants: An aggregate boundary should encapsulate only data that must be strictly consistent within a single • Rule 2: Design Small Aggregates: Large aggregates cause severe optimistic locking conflicts and memory bloat.

title: Entity vs Value Object Deep Dive.
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: Dimension Entity Value Object.

title: Domain Services vs Application Services.
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: Domain Service: Holds pure business logic that does not naturally belong to a single Entity or spans multiple Aggregate Roots (e.g • Application Service (Use Case Orchestrator): The outer boundary coordinator • Opens database transaction • Loads Aggregate from Repository.

title: Domain Events Lifecycle: Internal emission vs Outbox publishing.
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: How events travel from aggregate mutations to external message brokers: Emitted Inside Aggregate: Calling order.cancel("Customer request") records an internal event in an uncommitted in-memory list.

title: Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL) Architecture: Facade, Adapter, and Translator.
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: When your clean modern domain must communicate with a 20-year-old legacy SOAP mainframe: Never let the legacy system's confusing abbreviations (CUSTMSTRREC_01) leak into your clean domain model! • The ACL Trio • Facade: Simplifies the messy legacy API into a manageable interface.

title: Modeling Invariants: Eliminating public setters in Aggregate Roots.
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: Anemic Domain Anti-Pattern: Entities full of getters and public setters (order.setStatus("PAID"), order.setDiscount(0.2)) • Rich Domain Model: Private setters.

title: CQRS and Event Sourcing in DDD: State reconstruction and projections.
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: Event-Sourced Aggregate: Has zero internal update statements.

title: Factory Pattern in DDD: Enforcing invariants during object creation.
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: When creating an Aggregate Root requires complex business validation, loading child entities, or establishing initial invariants: Direct instantiation via new Order() can lead to partially configured or invalid domain objects • Domain Factory: Encapsulates atomic creation.

title: Integrating Legacy Systems: Bubble Contexts and Autonomous Bubbles.
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: When replacing a legacy system in phases: Bubble Context: A clean, isolated island of new development carved out inside or alongside the legacy architecture • Communicates with the legacy system strictly through an Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL).

title: Testing in DDD: Unit testing Domain Entities in pure isolation.
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: Because true Tactical DDD models have zero dependencies on databases, ORMs, frameworks, or networks: Domain unit tests execute in microseconds.

title: Socio-Technical Architecture: Aligning Team Topologies with Bounded Contexts.
part: Part 3: Advanced Architecture & Production Patterns (Senior / Lead)
summary: Conway's Law states: "Organizations design systems that mirror their own communication structures": If 3 separate teams work inside a single shared Bounded Context, they will suffer from constant merge conflicts, blocked deployments, and • Socio-Technical Alignment (Team Topologies).

title: What is System Design and What is the Standard 4-Step Framework for Technical Interviews?
part: Part 1: Foundational Distributed Systems Concepts & Trade-offs (1 - 10)
summary: System Design is the process of defining the architecture, components, modules, interfaces, and data for a system to satisfy specified business and technical requirements at scale.

title: Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling: Architectural Trade-offs and Bottlenecks.
part: Part 1: Foundational Distributed Systems Concepts & Trade-offs (1 - 10)
summary: Vertical Scaling (Scale-Up): Adding more CPU, RAM, or NVMe disk capacity to a single physical or virtual machine • Horizontal Scaling (Scale-Out): Adding more discrete commodity instances into a distributed pool behind a load balancer.

title: The CAP Theorem & PACELC Theorem Deep-Dive.
part: Part 1: Foundational Distributed Systems Concepts & Trade-offs (1 - 10)
summary: The CAP Theorem states that a distributed data store can guarantee at most two of three characteristics simultaneously in the presence of a network partition: Consistency (C): Every read receives the most recent write or an error.

title: Distributed Consistency Models: Strong, Eventual, Causal, and Read-Your-Writes.
part: Part 1: Foundational Distributed Systems Concepts & Trade-offs (1 - 10)
summary: Consistency models define the contract between a distributed storage system and its applications regarding the order and freshness of observed data across multiple nodes: Strong (Linearizable) Consistency: Once a write completes, all subsequent reads across all nodes immediately return that value or newer.

title: Load Balancing Algorithms and Layer 4 vs Layer 7 Reverse Proxies.
part: Part 1: Foundational Distributed Systems Concepts & Trade-offs (1 - 10)
summary: A Load Balancer (LB) distributes incoming network traffic across a cluster of backend servers to ensure high throughput, fault tolerance, and zero-downtime deployments.: Layer 4 Load Balancing (Transport Layer - TCP/UDP) • Operates on IP address and port numbers without inspecting application payload.

title: Consistent Hashing and Virtual Nodes: Mitigating Hot-Spots and Rebalancing.
part: Part 1: Foundational Distributed Systems Concepts & Trade-offs (1 - 10)
summary: In standard modulo hashing (hash(key) % N), adding or removing a single server forces almost 100% of keys to be relocated to new servers, causing catastrophic cache stampedes and database overloads. Consistent Hashing maps both servers and data keys onto a circular 2^{32}-1 hash ring.

title: Caching Strategies: Cache-Aside, Write-Through, Write-Behind, and Write-Around.
part: Part 1: Foundational Distributed Systems Concepts & Trade-offs (1 - 10)
summary: Caching reduces latency and offloads database IOPS by storing hot data in ultra-fast RAM (Redis/Memcached). The choice of caching pattern defines how reads and writes interact.

title: Cache Stampede, Thundering Herd, and Cache Invalidation Strategies.
part: Part 1: Foundational Distributed Systems Concepts & Trade-offs (1 - 10)
summary: Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd): When a heavily requested hot cache key expires (e.g. homepage top stories or flash sale product), thousands of • Cache Penetration: Malicious or buggy clients query keys that exist neither in cache nor in the database (e.g. id = -9999), constantly hitting the DB.

title: Message Brokers vs Event Streaming: RabbitMQ vs Apache Kafka.
part: Part 1: Foundational Distributed Systems Concepts & Trade-offs (1 - 10)
summary: Message Broker (RabbitMQ) • Smart broker, dumb consumer model • Messages are pushed to consumers via AMQP • Once acknowledged (ACK), messages are deleted from the broker.

title: Database Sharding Strategies: Range, Hash, and Directory-Based Partitioning.
part: Part 1: Foundational Distributed Systems Concepts & Trade-offs (1 - 10)
summary: Sharding is the horizontal partitioning of a large database across multiple independent physical database instances (shards) when a single database exceeds memory, storage, or connection limits.

title: Design a Distributed URL Shortener (TinyURL / Bit.ly).
part: Part 2: Real-World High-Scale Architecture Problems (11 - 25)
summary: Design a scalable service that converts long URLs (e.g. 150 characters) into concise aliases (e.g. https://tiny.cc/a8X9k2) and redirects users with sub-15ms latency.

title: Design a Distributed Rate Limiter.
part: Part 2: Real-World High-Scale Architecture Problems (11 - 25)
summary: Protect backend microservices from DDoS attacks, brute-force bots, and resource starvation by enforcing request quota policies (e.g. 100 requests per minute per IP or API key). Algorithm Comparison: Token Bucket (Optimal): Tokens are added to a bucket at a constant refill rate.

title: Design a Real-Time Chat System (WhatsApp / Slack / Discord).
part: Part 2: Real-World High-Scale Architecture Problems (11 - 25)
summary: Support 1-on-1 private messaging, group channels, persistent chat history, and online status with end-to-end delivery guarantees. Core Components: Connection Handshake: Client connects via HTTP/HTTPS, authenticates, and upgrades connection to bidirectional WebSocket.

title: Design Twitter / Social Media Feed System (Fan-Out on Write vs Fan-Out on Read).
part: Part 2: Real-World High-Scale Architecture Problems (11 - 25)
summary: Design an interactive timeline where users can post tweets (tweets/sec: 10K writes) and view a personalized chronological feed of tweets from accounts they follow (feeds/sec: 500K reads). The Architectural Dilemma: Fan-Out on Write vs Fan-Out on Read: Fan-Out on Write (Push Model).

title: Design a Proximity / Ride-Sharing Service (Uber / Lyft).
part: Part 2: Real-World High-Scale Architecture Problems (11 - 25)
summary: Connect drivers with nearby riders in real-time while processing location updates every 4 seconds from millions of active vehicles with sub-100ms spatial matching. Spatial Indexing Technologies: Geohash: Hierarchical spatial data structure that subdivides Earth into bounding grid boxes and encodes them into Base32 strings.

title: Design a Global Video Streaming Platform (YouTube / Netflix).
part: Part 2: Real-World High-Scale Architecture Problems (11 - 25)
summary: Ingest raw video files uploaded by creators, transcode them into multiple resolutions and bitrates, and stream playback smoothly to diverse devices across variable network bandwidths. Core Architecture & Streaming Protocols: HLS (HTTP Live Streaming) / MPEG-DASH • Videos are split into small chunks (2–6 seconds each).

title: Design a Distributed Unique ID Generator (Twitter Snowflake ID).
part: Part 2: Real-World High-Scale Architecture Problems (11 - 25)
summary: Generate unique 64-bit integer IDs across thousands of distributed servers without requiring centralized database auto-increments or slow distributed consensus coordination. Snowflake 64-Bit Structure: 1 bit: Unused sign bit (always 0) • 41 bits: Timestamp in milliseconds since custom epoch (2^{41} approx 69 years of IDs).

title: Design a Distributed Web Crawler (URL Frontier, Bloom Filters, and Politeness).
part: Part 2: Real-World High-Scale Architecture Problems (11 - 25)
summary: Systematically crawl billions of web pages across the public internet for indexing, processing 100,000 pages per second while adhering to host politeness policies (robots.txt).

title: Design an Idempotent Payment System (Stripe / Checkout).
part: Part 2: Real-World High-Scale Architecture Problems (11 - 25)
summary: Ensure that double-clicks, network timeouts, or retried API calls NEVER charge a customer twice or corrupt bank transaction balances. Idempotency Key Architecture: Client generates a UUIDv4 Idempotency Key in request header (Idempotency-Key: c9d721...) • Payment gateway acquires a distributed lock in Redis for that key.

title: Design a Cloud File Storage & Synchronization Service (Google Drive / Dropbox).
part: Part 2: Real-World High-Scale Architecture Problems (11 - 25)
summary: Allow users to upload, download, and synchronize files of arbitrary size across desktop and mobile devices with automatic delta sync and data deduplication. Core Innovations: Chunking (Delta Sync): Files are divided into 4MB chunks • Content-Addressable Storage: Each chunk is named after its SHA-256 hash.

title: Design a Typeahead / Autocomplete Search System (Trie & Top-K Ranking).
part: Part 2: Real-World High-Scale Architecture Problems (11 - 25)
summary: Provide real-time query suggestions as the user types each keystroke into a search bar within 30ms latency, handling 50,000 keystrokes per second.

title: Design a Distributed Notification Service (APNs, FCM, SMS, and Email).
part: Part 2: Real-World High-Scale Architecture Problems (11 - 25)
summary: Send billions of push notifications, SMS texts, and transactional emails with high delivery rates, user notification preferences, and deduplication. Architectural Highlights: Notification Template Engine: Renders dynamic strings and localized language templates.

title: Design an E-Commerce Flash Sale System (High Concurrency & Inventory Reservation).
part: Part 2: Real-World High-Scale Architecture Problems (11 - 25)
summary: Prevent overselling when 500,000 customers try to purchase 1,000 limited-stock gaming consoles within 3 seconds of a flash sale launch. The Solution: Atomic In-Memory Inventory Reservation: Relational database row locks (SELECT .. • Pattern: Preload inventory into Redis Decr or Lua script.

title: Design a Distributed Key-Value Store (Dynamo-Style Vector Clocks & Gossip Protocol).
part: Part 2: Real-World High-Scale Architecture Problems (11 - 25)
summary: Design an Amazon Dynamo-style highly available, partition-tolerant distributed key-value store with eventual consistency and decentralized masterless architecture. Key Technical Pillars: Decentralized Membership: Nodes monitor cluster health via Gossip Protocol (epidemic information dissemination).

title: Design a Web Analytics / Event Tracking Platform (Kafka + ClickHouse / Druid).
part: Part 2: Real-World High-Scale Architecture Problems (11 - 25)
summary: Ingest, aggregate, and query 10 billion daily user interaction events (pageviews, clicks, scroll depth) with real-time dashboard visualization. Storage Architecture: Columnar vs Row-Oriented: Row-oriented databases (PostgreSQL/MySQL) are designed for single-row OLTP operations.

title: Distributed Consensus: Raft vs Paxos.
part: Part 3: Distributed Transactions, Consensus & Reliability (26 - 36)
summary: Distributed consensus algorithms ensure that a cluster of servers agree on a shared state machine log, even if some nodes crash or experience network partitions.: Paxos: The original consensus algorithm proven by Leslie Lamport • Raft: Designed specifically to be understandable while providing equivalent safety to Multi-Paxos.

title: Two-Phase Commit (2PC) vs Three-Phase Commit (3PC).
part: Part 3: Distributed Transactions, Consensus & Reliability (26 - 36)
summary: Atomic transaction protocols that ensure all participating database nodes either commit or abort a distributed transaction together.: Two-Phase Commit (2PC) • Phase 1 (Prepare): Coordinator asks all participants: "Can you commit?" Participants lock resources and respond YES/NO.

title: The Saga Pattern: Orchestration vs Choreography for Microservices.
part: Part 3: Distributed Transactions, Consensus & Reliability (26 - 36)
summary: In microservice architectures where each service owns its private database, ACID multi-database transactions are anti-patterns. A Saga is a sequence of local transactions where each step publishes an event. If any step fails, the Saga executes Compensating Transactions backwards to undo previous actions.

title: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) & Event Sourcing.
part: Part 3: Distributed Transactions, Consensus & Reliability (26 - 36)
summary: CQRS: Separates the data model for write modifications (Commands) from read queries (Queries) • Event Sourcing: Instead of storing only the current state of an entity, every state change is stored as an immutable append-only event log.

title: Distributed Locking: Redlock Algorithm vs ZooKeeper / etcd.
part: Part 3: Distributed Transactions, Consensus & Reliability (26 - 36)
summary: Coordinate exclusive access to a shared resource across multiple independent compute instances.: Redis Redlock: Acquires lock across N independent Redis masters (typically 5) • ZooKeeper / etcd: Uses consensus-backed ephemeral sequential nodes.

title: Gossip Protocols and Cluster Membership Discovery.
part: Part 3: Distributed Transactions, Consensus & Reliability (26 - 36)
summary: A decentralized peer-to-peer communication protocol where nodes periodically exchange membership and liveness state with a small set of random peers, spreading information exponentially like an epidemic.: Used by Apache Cassandra, Amazon DynamoDB, and HashiCorp Consul.

title: Resolving Concurrent Write Conflicts: Last-Write-Wins (LWW) vs CRDTs.
part: Part 3: Distributed Transactions, Consensus & Reliability (26 - 36)
summary: When two users update the identical key concurrently across partitioned nodes: Last-Write-Wins (LWW): Uses wall-clock NTP timestamp • Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs): Mathematically proven data structures (e.g. G-Counter, PN-Counter, OR-Set) that converge to the.

title: Circuit Breaker Pattern (Netflix Hystrix / Resilience4j).
part: Part 3: Distributed Transactions, Consensus & Reliability (26 - 36)
summary: Prevent cascading failures when a downstream microservice is down. Instead of exhausting worker threads on blocking timeouts, the Circuit Breaker trips to OPEN state and fails fast.: CLOSED: Requests flow normally • OPEN: Error threshold exceeded • HALF-OPEN: After sleep window, allows trial requests.

title: Dead Letter Queues (DLQ) and Exponential Backoff with Full Jitter.
part: Part 3: Distributed Transactions, Consensus & Reliability (26 - 36)
summary: When retrying failed network calls or message processing, retrying immediately causes thundering herd traffic spikes.: Exponential Backoff: Multiplies sleep interval by 2^n on each failure (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, 16s...).

title: Database Replication Lag, Split-Brain & Leader Election.
part: Part 3: Distributed Transactions, Consensus & Reliability (26 - 36)
summary: Replication Lag: Time elapsed between a write committing to the Leader and replicating to Followers • Split-Brain: When a network partition divides a cluster into two isolated subnets, and both subnets elect their own Leader and accept • Fix: Strict Majority Quorum (N/2 + 1).

title: Zero-Downtime Database Migrations (Expand and Contract Pattern).
part: Part 3: Distributed Transactions, Consensus & Reliability (26 - 36)
summary: How to rename columns or alter schemas on live production databases with billions of rows without table locks or service downtime.: Expand: Add new nullable column newcolumn • Dual-Write: Deploy application code that reads from oldcolumn and writes to both oldcolumn and newcolumn.

title: REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC: Serialization, Latency & Streaming Trade-offs.
part: Part 4: API Design, Security & Edge Networking (37 - 43)
summary: REST: Standard over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 using JSON • GraphQL: Client specifies exact fields needed, eliminating over-fetching and under-fetching • gRPC: Uses Protocol Buffers (binary serialization) over HTTP/2 multiplexing.

title: The API Gateway Pattern: Authentication, Rate Limiting & Aggregation.
part: Part 4: API Design, Security & Edge Networking (37 - 43)
summary: A single reverse-proxy entry point for all client requests that handles cross-cutting concerns: SSL termination, JWT authentication, rate limiting, request tracing, and payload aggregation.

title: WebSockets vs Server-Sent Events (SSE) vs Long Polling.
part: Part 4: API Design, Security & Edge Networking (37 - 43)
summary: WebSockets: Full-duplex bidirectional TCP communication • Server-Sent Events (SSE): Unidirectional server-to-client streaming over standard HTTP • Long Polling: Legacy fallback where client holds an HTTP request open until the server responds.

title: Content Delivery Networks (CDNs): Edge Caching & Anycast Routing.
part: Part 4: API Design, Security & Edge Networking (37 - 43)
summary: Geographically distributed network of proxy servers that cache static assets and dynamic responses close to end users.: Anycast BGP: Routes client DNS queries to the topologically nearest physical datacenter • Cache-Control Headers: s-maxage, stale-while-revalidate, and instant tag purging.

title: Distributed Tracing & W3C TraceContext (OpenTelemetry).
part: Part 4: API Design, Security & Edge Networking (37 - 43)
summary: Track a single end-user request as it traverses across dozens of microservices.: Trace ID: Unique identifier for the entire request journey • Span ID: Identifies individual unit of work in a specific service • Baggage: Context propagated across HTTP/gRPC boundaries via W3C traceparent headers.

title: DDoS Attack Mitigation: SYN Flood, Slowloris & Anycast Absorption.
part: Part 4: API Design, Security & Edge Networking (37 - 43)
summary: SYN Flood (Layer 4): Floods TCP SYN packets without sending final ACK to exhaust connection memory table • Slowloris (Layer 7): Sends HTTP headers at agonizingly slow rates to keep server thread pool occupied • Anycast Absorption: Distributes massive attack volume across hundreds of edge locations worldwide.

title: TLS 1.3 Handshake & Zero Round-Trip Time (0-RTT) Resumption.
part: Part 4: API Design, Security & Edge Networking (37 - 43)
summary: TLS 1.3 reduces the handshake from two round-trips (2-RTT in TLS 1.2) to a single round-trip (1-RTT). 0-RTT Resumption allows returning clients to send encrypted application data in the very first flight.

title: Latency Numbers Every Software Engineer Should Know.
part: Part 5: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation & Production Calculations (44 - 50)
summary: Approximate physical hardware latencies that dictate architectural trade-offs.
